Mr. G. R. GEARY (South Toronto) moved the second reading of Bill No. 15, to incorporate the Small Loan Company of Canada.
Explain.

This is a bill which I have introduced at the request of a very reputable set of people. While I know very little about it myself I am advised that it follows in its terms precisely the bill that was passed by this house last year. This bill has to do with the making of small loans on personal security. I am aware that there was some objection made to the bill last year, but as far as I am advised there was no change made therein, and I am also told that, the superintendent of insurance approved the principle and thought that such companies as these were of some use in the community as they absorbed the pressure to get small loans rather than large loans, and loans on personal property rather than on real property.
TMr. Bennett.]
Is this bill to be referred to the private bills committee, may I ask?
It will go to that committee, I suppose.

I would like to make two observations upon the second reading of this bill. My first observation is that we have a bill before the house setting up a central bank, and therefore I do not see the necessity of incorporating the Small Loan Company of Canada.
My second observation is a more serious one. We all remember the Stavisky scandal in France which came about through the bankruptcy of a corporation of this very kind. Parliament should be very careful about incorporating small loan companies in Canada. I have always advised my electors to be prudent in these matters. I do not see why these gentlemen should come to parliament for a bill of this kind because there are loaning facilities in every branch of every chartered bank in Canada. These chartered banks come under the department of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), and there is a very thorough inspection of them, while the small loan companies are not subjected to the same inspection and care. If we give this bill its second reading I am afraid that people might go throughout the country selling shares of this corporation, just as they have done in the case of other companies, stealing the people's money and holding out to them the prospect of making huge profits if they invest in such a scheme. We know these birds of prey who tour the country urging the people to invest their money in such and such a scheme which the promoters say will produce for the people a profit of 25 and sometimes 50 per cent a year. But what happens? If a man subscribes $500 in such a scheme they cash his cheque and give him back $250 the same day and tell him, "Here is your profit, and you are getting it back the same day that you invested your money." Then they decamp with the other $250 and he never sees them again until the police catch them.
There was a finance corporation that failed in Toronto a few years ago. I am not against finance. I am not against the lending of money to poor people, but I do not like what we call in French "prets a la petite semaine"-that Shylock method of lending money to individuals.
Companies of this sort ask all kinds of guarantees. We do not know anything about any of these people. They may be honest.

Small Loan Company
We may give them the benefit of the doubt and say that they might be honest but perhaps they are not, and it is my duty, representing not only my county but the Canadian people in this parliament, to advise my colleagues to be very careful about companies of this kind, and also to ask my hon. colleagues in this house not to let this bill pass without first of all scrutinizing it very thoroughly. Otherwise the people will say, "It is you, the House of Commons and the Senate, which passed this legislation giving these people the chance to cut the flesh of our fellow-citizens." I do not see the necessity for this bill. I do not know any of these people. I am always ready to oblige anyone who comes here with decent legislation, and perhaps this is decent legislation, but perhaps it is not. We need more information, and I would ask the hon. gentleman who has moved the second reading of this bill to delay before pressing for a vote on the second reading so that we may get more information.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose the second reading of this bill. I would call the attention of hon. members of the house to just two or three points before they vote on the second reading.
First of all, I would ask them to read section five of the bill andi to note that paragraph (b) of that section provides that-
Read the section.

It is a long section, and the hon. member has the bill before him. Paragraph (b) provides:
Notwithstanding anything contained in the Interest Act, or in the Money Lenders Act, or in paragraph (c) of section sixty-three of the Loan Companies Act,
-this company may do certain things which the section goes on to enumerate. I just wish to point out to the house that these various acts mentioned and section sixty-three of the Loan Companies Act were passed for the very purpose which the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has pointed out, for the protection of the people of this dominion, and that they have been on the statute books for many years. I am of the opinion, regardless of what the promoter of this bill may say, that we have quite enough of these small loan companies acts, and perhaps too many already, and the time has come when we should scrutinize them with a great deal more particularity than we have done in the past.
I would also call attention to subsection (i) of section five which permits the company to lend on various types of securities, and I would particularly ask hon. gentlemen to note that although subsection (i) of section five provides that the interest rate may not be more than seven per cent, this interest is deducted at the time the loan is made, and that the amount loaned is payable weekly, monthly or per annum as it may be provided, aind so at the very end of the first month there is an overlapping of interest, and before the loan is finally paid off the party borrowing has paid very much more than seven per cent interest.
The next subsection (ii), marginally noted, Charges for Expenses, provides that two per cent .upon the principal of the loan may be charged by the company for expenses. That makes nine per cent, and more as I have already pointed out.
The next subsection (iii) provides that there may be an additional charge. This subsection provides that for the drawing of a chattel mortgage which they take upon the various chattels as security they may charge an additional $10 regardless of the size of the loan. This is exorbitant, and I protest and ask the house, if they decide that this bill shall go to the private bills committee, to see that the whole bill be very carefully scrutinized in order that the general public may be protected.

Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to agree with the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, although I am not unmindful of the fact that in days gone by similar charters have been granted by this parliament. In those days I protested against the granting of charters which gave to a company powers of the character mentioned in this bill. Surely the days of usury are past; if the chartered banks of this country are to be limited to six and seven per cent by action of this parliament, this same parliament should not set up a company which can charge forty per cent. Personally, I think it would be fair to have this bill go to the private bills, the banking and commerce or some other appropriate committee but I think this parliament should pause and consider before there is created under the imprimatur of this and the other house a corporation which will be able to do what this bill will permit it to do. I feel like voting against the second reading but if it is the sense of the house that this bill should go to a committee, well and good. Personally, I do not think we have room in this country for
Small Loan Company

this class of company although I am bound to say that the superintendent of insurance has stated before committees of this house that this class of corporation fills a need in the community. I never agreed with him and I propose to vote against the second reading.

Mr. Speaker, we have on our files a bill to create a central bank of Canada and another one to revise the Bank Act of Canada. These bills are intended to revise the whole financial system of Canada. Under the circumstances, I think this is the proper time for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and the government to step in and hold up this bill until they have learned from the action taken in connection with the other bills just what is the feeling of this house. I think this should be done before any further legislation of this character is permitted to pass.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to add my
opposition to this bill. The hon. member who introduced it (Mr. Geary) has referred to the fact that already similar companies are in existence. I do not think that is sufficient justification for the creation of this company and, in fact, I think we should give serious consideration to putting some curb upon those already in existence. I 'have in my office at the present time an illustration of where one of these companies has been receiving until recently one hundred per cent on their investment, mainly through what they call a financing charge. I think the time has come when this type of legislation should be gome into. We should not encourage the people to buy that for which they cannot afford to pay, and that is what this type of financing is supposed to do. I do not think I can agree with the hon. member who has suggested that we should allow this bill to go to committee; I think we should take a vote upon it right now and kill it immediately. If the hon. member wants to reconsider his bill and bring it up in another form which will put some limit upon the financing and other unreasonable charges, perhaps I might change my mind. I do not say that I am against any particular bill but I am against this type of legislation and I think this bill should be killed right now.

there is something more in this bill than simply the principle, to incorporate a company. It is the principle permitting it to do business along the lines indicated in the bill. The promoters could be heard.

Small Loan Company

It is only a matter of less than an hour since a public bill was dealt with in, a very different way. That bill was killed on the first reading before members had a chance to consider it. That bill could have gone to a committee which committee could have received suggestions from the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) as to what changes should be made in order to bring it into harmony with the policies of the government. This procedure was not followed in the case of a public bill involving large numbers of our fellow Canadians and I do not see why it should be taken in the case of a company which asks for power to do business by methods which are generally believed to be not in keeping with the welfare of this country. I do not see why this bill should be put forward one stage.

I oppose this bill for all the reasons which have been put forward and for another one as well. A great number of these small loan companies have received charters from the provincial governments and I do not see why this company should not make application to the government of Ontario for authority to do business in that province. They could then take their chances of being permitted to do business in the other provinces of Canada. They are now endeavouring to get the privilege of doing business in every province of Canada willynilly. I am against the principle of this bill and I intend to oppose it altogether. I know that the government proposes to bring in legislation to exercise some restraint upon these companies but heretofore such restraint has not been imposed and that is why such companies come to the federal government for their charters. For this reason more than any other I am opposing the second reading of this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the reason such companies come to the federal government for charters is not to evade the requirements of any provincial legislation as they cannot operate or do business in any province of Canada without first obtaining a provincial licence under the terms of the provincial act.
Other companies have been doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rise to speak with regard to this bill because I notice that the prov-visional directors named in the bill represent a family in the city of Guelph, which is one of the best known families in the Dominion of Canada. The head of their family at the
present time is Mr. Arthur Cutten of Chicago. This company will not prove a minor or temporary institution. It will be a most substantial undertaking with a million dollars of capital which will be largely if not altogether under the control of members of the Cutten family. This fact alone should be a sufficient answer to much of the criticism which has been offered upon this motion.
Ail the promoters ask in this motion is that this bill be read a second time and go to the appropriate committee. It may be sent to the private bills committee or it may be sent to the banking and commerce committee, I care not which; but when it goes to the committee the promoters of the bill are entitled to appear and state their case- they cannot appear in this house. The committee may incorporate in the bill such conditions or stipulations with respect to the operations of the company as it may see fit. But surely, having advertised this bill as required by law, having paid the fee as required by law, having properly brought the bill before parliament, the promoters are entitled to be heard in the fullest manner. That is all that the second reading of the bill involves. The bill will be fully under the control of whatever committee it is referred to, and any amendments the committee deems proper to place in the bill may be embodied in it. Subsequently it will be referred back to the house and the house in committee will again deal with it. I submit that the bill should be read the second time and sent to the appropriate committee so that it may be given the fullest consideration.

If the house divides I shall have to vote to send the bill to the committee, because I agree with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) in the observations he has made. But in voting that way I should add a word of explanation, because, with the other hon. members who have spoken with respect to the operation of these companies, I am in thorough agreement. I know that in the part of Canada from which I come there is a great deal of complaint with respect to the operation of these companies that make small loans, and I respectfully suggest to the house and the government that possibly some steps should be taken to bring these companies a little more into line with what the public expects them to be.
It may be said that the provincial companies are incorporated by provincial law, but this parliament has jurisdiction over interest and interest rates, and it is high time
Small Loan Company

that the basis of operation of this particular type of company be looked into. I shall vote to send the bill to the committee, if the house divides, but in doing so I want it understood that I am fully sensible of the objections to the measure.

I strongly object to this bill, and one of my chief reasons for objecting is the vote taken a little while ago on the bill that was presented by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). A gentleman presents a bill which affects the lives of many people, those liable to be separated from their families, and,-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. My reason for voting against this bill is this. The Minister of Justice said that these people had spent their money and that the custom of the house was to have such bills read the second time and sent to the committee on banking and commerce to be reviewed, so that its promoters might have an opportunity .to appear and state their case. But this is my objection-and I think I am in order in the statement I am about to make. How can I vote either for or against a bill I have never seen? Yet this house votes against the principle of allowing bills to be introduced. I do not see any consistency in such action.
The present motion is for the second reading of the bill; the first reading was carried.

No doubt the first reading was carried, Mr. Speaker, but the principle is the same. Now, may I say that in my opinion we have too many of these loan companies who have gone about the country fleecing people who know nothing about finance. We have had such companies in Winnipeg. There was one music company that fleeced everyone it came in contact with; it had no other object than that. If you vote for the second reading of this bill you vote for the principle of it, as far as I understand the rules. If you refer the bill to a committee you are virtually saying, by a majority vote of this house, that you approve of the principle laid down in the bill, and I am opposed to it.

I will vote against the second reading of this bill, for a reason not yet stated in the house. It seems to me that the purpose of the bill is the creation of a pawnshop-a pawnshop similar to the one that caused so much trouble in France. You will be convinced of that if you read the beginning of section 5 of the bill. I have not my English file before me, but in French it reads:
(1) La compagnie pent, dans tout le Canada:
(a) acheter. vendre et negocier des contrats de vente conditionnelle, des billets de creances priviligiees, des contrats de vente a temperament, des hypotheques mobilieres-

Small Loan Company
The English version reads:
The company may throughout Canada:
(a) buy, sell, deal in and lend money on the security of conditional sales agreements, lien notes, hire purchase agreements, chattel mortgages-
Chattel mortgages are prohibited in Quebec by the civil code.

trade paper, bills of lading, warehouse receipts, bills of exchange and choses-in-aetion; and may receive and accept from the makers, vendors or transferors thereof guarantees or other security for the performance and payment thereof and may enforce such guarantees and realize on such security.
The purpose of the bill is to authorize the company to loan money on chattel mortgages and on movable property pawned with them, and therefore the purpose of the bill is the creation of nothing else but a pawnshop. And we have already too many of these pawnshops.

It seems
to me that the very fact that these gentlemen come before parliament and ask for the powers enumerated in this bill would indicate that they intend to use those powers if they get an opportunity, and the powers asked for include the charging of higher rates than the law allows. Now, when men deliberately declare that this is their intention they should not be encouraged to go into the loaning business.

I
rise to oppose the second reading of this bill. It is true that we have some similar measures on the statute books, but companies have of late years attempted to get similar bills through this house and on two occasions that I know of they have been defeated. Only a year or so ago we had one very similar bill before the banking and commerce committee, and we then thought it was not in the best interests of the country to pass it. I trust this bill will not get second reading.

While
I am opposed to the enactment of any legislation of this kind for the reasons given, I have always believed that a bill should never be killed before it reaches a committee. In my parliamentary experience the attitude I have always assumed is that any bill properly introduced before the house should receive its first and second readings, go to committee and there have its merits threshed out. speechtext:

In this country we have quite a few advocates of silver. Some hon. members of this house, including the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), have at various times advocated the rehabilitation of silver. The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, as far back as 1931, also made this statement:
I can assure you that I am more and more convinced, as time goes on, that the fundamental cause of our present difficulty is really monetary, and that it is the penalty for a long-pursued and very stupid policy of unduly forcing the gold standard and driving silver-the medium of exchange of half the world-into such low price levels as to paralyze the buying powers of hundreds of millions of humanity. There seems to be no leadership in the present situation at all, and it will have to soon develop or troubles political will follow on troubles commercial.
There is also another prominent advocate of silver in the person of Father Coughlin of the United States, who according to press dispatches, has, it is estimated, more than a million followers who believe that silver should be recognized and accepted as a legal base with gold.
In the limited time at my disposal I cannot go very fully into all the "whereases " of my resolution, but I think it is a fair statement that each "whereas" clause is a statement of fact, and I believe of actual history.
Take the first "whereas":
Whereas, goods or services between nations or people can only be paid for either by other goods or services, or by some unit of value acceptable to those desiring such goods or services, and which unit of value has for ages been the precious metals, silver and gold;
I do not think any hon. member will disagree with that statement. Then I come to the second clause:
And whereas, for centuries past, silver was the only precious metal used, both as currency and as the unit of value for the interchange of goods iand services;
In regard to that I think everyone in the house who has given the matter even a casual examination must realize that in the early stages of mankind's history barter, the exchange of goods for goods, was the first medium of exchange. But early in the history of the world barter was discarded, and man adopted one or other of the precious metals, particularly silver. The history of silver goes away back to Bible times. In Genesis, chapter 23, it is recorded that Abraham bought a field for burying his

people, and in the sixteenth verse of that chapter we are told that he paid four hundred shekels of silver in current money for that field. That is going a long way back and I mention it to show that silver has been used from the very earliest times. Right on down through the ages, through Anglo-Saxon times and down to the eighteenth century, silver has been used. It is true that gold was also used, but silver was the chief medium of exchange and it had its price to gold; in other words, it was a case of gold to silver, not silver to gold. In fact, the pound sterling was based on the price of one pound of silver. One pound of silver was recognized as one pound sterling, and hence we have the term sterling silver.
We come to the year 1717, when Great Britain was the first nation to adopt what we call to-day bimetallism. In that year Great Britain added gold as primary currency to silver. In 1816 a change was however made. Great Britain for the first time in its history, and for the first time in the history of the world, I believe, went on the gold standard. That change was made not because silver had failed or was inadequate but for this reason, as given by those who have delved into such matters:	The bankers, especially
the Rothschilds, controlled the debt after the Napoleonic wars and so benefited by the change to gold. At that time Great Britain was starting in upon her industrial era, and she could therefore purchase more goods abroad in silver countries by purchasing on the single standard of gold. After the act of 1816 she had what is known as a bimetallic standard.
In 1870, after the Franco-Prussian war, Germany compelled France to pay her debts in gold, Germany reaping thereby a great benefit by adopting gold as the single standard.
In 1873 we have the United States discontinuing her silver currency and going on to the gold standard.
I have touched very briefly on these periods, Mr. Speaker, as they are outstanding in any discussion of this subject. I would ask the house to take note that those three periods I have mentioned, 1816, 1870 and 1873, when the bankers of the world compelled the different countries to go on the gold standard and discard silver as the prime metal, were periods of great distress.
We come along to the year 1920, in our own times. Gold has always been an obsession with the Bank of England. In 1920 international bankers met at Berne and there decided to go on gold and to discard silver

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Reid
entirely. As a matter of fact, Germany in that year was offered gold by international bankers so that she also could go on the gold standard. The price of silver in that year was a little over one dollar an ounce. Gold was at a discount. From 1920-1921 the demonetization of silver started. Great Britain I believe was the first country to demonetize silver, although there is some doubt regarding that, some authorities stating that the United States first started it by demonetizing her silver. These authorities say that Great Britain was the first. Great Britain and the United States, either jointly or following one another, started to debase or demonetize their silver coinage and it was not long before other countries of the world followed suit. In 1925 Great Britain purchased from the United States 260,000,000 silver dollars. These were taken to the old country and melted down. There were added
200,000,000 ounces of copper and from this mixture was fabricated a counterfeit or false coin containing 50 per cent silver and 50 per cent copper. The purer silver coins had been gradually called in and these were melted down and the resultant silver dumped on the Chinese market. It was during this year that the break took place in the price of silver.
Great Britain then went a little further. Two years later she issued a makeshift paper currency for the 350,000,000 people of India. She melted down one billion rupees and issued one billion rupees in paper. When this amount of silver was thrown on the world's markets the price broke to the lowest it had even been. Not only did Great Britain do this but she compelled the Indian government to place a tax of 11 cents per ounce against silver in an effort to stop an influx of silver into that country. I should like to quote from a United States Department of Commerce bulletin, issued in 1933 and referring to a committee which investigated this matter of debasement. One paragraph reads as follows:
According to the sixty-first annual report of the deputy master and comptroller of the Royal Mint for 1930, the weight of the silver coinage withdrawn during the ten years was about
6,000	tons. One can estimate the approximate weight of silver in this amount, which would be about 5,550 tons, or 181,258,560 ounces. The weight of the new coins minted is given in the above-mentioned report as about 4,800 tons. Estimating from this figure, it would appear that the silver content, which would be about 2,400 tons, represents about 78,382,080 ounces. Thus there appears to have been, during the ten years, a surplus balance of about 3,150 tons, or about 102,876,480 ounces.
It is estimated that in the world to-day there is over $6,000,000,000 of debased silver
coinage. Like other countries, Canada followed the lead of Great Britain. It might be interesting to the house to know that until 1920 the silver coins issued by Canada were what is known as -925 fine or, in other words, 9| tenths pure. In 1920 a change was made and from then on the silver content was reduced to -800 which is 8 tenths fine. To-day an ounce of silver minted into Canadian coins produces $1.60 of coinage. Taking silver as being worth forty cents an ounce, for forty cents worth of silver the government issues $1.60 in Canadian coins. I give this illustration as I want to put before the house a clear picture of this matter and endeavour if possible to make my resolution more plain.
The short time at my disposal does not permit me to give the full details of the manipulations of the bankers but in these few remarks I hope I have shown that the monetary system now existing in the world has not been brought about by chance but by straight manipulation by the bankers of the world. It is the worship of the golden calf, and each monetary manipulation has been followed by long periods of low prices, distress and extreme poverty. Clause 4 of the resolution reads:
And whereas, the adoption of trade barriers and restrictions by many nations coupled with the very limited amount of gold available in the world for the interchange of goods and services has in large measure contributed to, if not brought about the unemployment of millions of people with its consequent untold misery and suffering;
I do not think any hon. member will deny the assertion that the adoption of trade barriers and restrictions by many nations coupled with the very limited amount of gold has in a large measure brought about the economic distress which prevails throughout the entire world. I should like to give a few figures with regard to the limitation of gold. It is estimated that in the world to-day there is a total of $12,000,000,000 in gold. This is held by practically three nations, the United States, France and Great Britain; 250,000,000 people own practically all the gold while
1,600,000,000 people have none. As someone has said, this is just like a poker game where all the chips are held by three players. The world's current debt is estimated at $750,000,000,000 which is a ratio of seventy-five to one to the gold held. The interest on this debt at five per cent amounts to $37,500,000,000, The debt of the world to the United States alone is $12,500,000,000. Why delude ourselves about the so-called gold standard when forty nations have abandoned it? Can anyone favour a return of that standard without a redistribution of gold? A few years ago the
Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Reid

trade of the world was estimated at $68,000,000,000 although it has now dropped to some-think like $28,000,000,000. Trade cannot be carried on against the present tariff barriers which exist plus the shortage which there now is of the one unit of value in use to-day, namely, gold. It has been said that modern engineers cannot conceive of the methods by which the pyramids were erected, but I think we have surpassed even that great feat. We are attempting to balance a pyramid of debt and trade on its apex instead of on its base. I do not think there is any doubt that trade restrictions and lack of gold have contributed to the unemployment and misery which we now have. Clause 5 reads:
And whereas, due to economic and existing monetary conditions many thousands of Canadian citizens have had to be sustained or given employment by the state;
I need hardly dwell on this phase of the matter because it has been brought out amply that there is in Canada over half a million people who are unemployed and well over a million who are being kept by the state. Clause 6 reads:
And whereas, Canada has been borrowing large sums to provide for the relief of the unemployed and destitute;
I think it was the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who stated that $173,000,000 has been expended by the dominion government on relief. A return was tabled the other day by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in which it is stated that the province of Manitoba owes over $6,000,000, the province of British Columbia over $7,000,000 and the province of Alberta over $8,000,000, all borrowed for the relief of unemployment or the borrowings made necessary by the lack of employment.
Clause 7 reads:
And whereas the issuing of currency in Canada has been based on certain coverage of gold, thereby restricting the amount of currency issued

I do not think anyone will refute that assertion, nor is it necessary for me to say a great deal regarding it. I am sure that everyone has seen the figures in this connection and knows that the total amount of gold in the country is roughly $70,000,000, whereas the notes outstanding against it amount to $184,427,058, or a coverage of gold of 40 per cent. In fact, I think the banking and commerce committee puts the coverage at exactly 38 per cent.
I come now to the resolution itself, which I will read:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government take immediate steps to adopt silver

in addition to that of gold for the issuance of currency either in the form of paper certificates or as coinage, and that silver be again recognized and accepted as legal tender by the Dominion of Canada at a fixed ratio to that of gold.
In dealing with this proposed resolution I wish to make my position clear with regard to the suggestion that Canada should adopt silver. Personally I am one of those who fear uncontrolled inflation. Those who have read history must realize that no nation can turn on the printing presses and survive, at least without great distress to the people, and especially the common people. I realize that as a cure the printing press cannot be turned on. But if the world must use precious metals I maintain that we should have silver in addition to gold. Certain efforts are being made in the great country to the south of us in connection with gold, but I believe that gold alone will not raise prices, and what is just as desirable to-day is the stabilization of currency. I claim that both these are impossible without the use of silver and especially in order to retain confidence and stability.
Before proceeding very far with the resolution itself I want to dicuss arguments that are sometimes made against the use of silver. One argument frequently heard is that if a country adopted silver as currency that country would be flooded with silver. That this is unfounded and grossly exaggerated I will show by certain figures which I am going to put on Hansard relative to the amount of silver in some countries of the world to-day. Some historians, especially those who have gone into the question of silver, have totalled up the amount produced in the world since the fourteenth century and it is estimated that a total of 14 billion ounces of silver has been produced. But the average world production of silver has run, between the years 1914 and 1930, at around 250 million ounces. In 1914 it was 178,331,433 ounces and in 1930 it was 245,788,030. But taking the average for a span of years it is safe to say that the average world production runs between 225 million and 250 million ounces of silver. The ratio has often been quoted as 16 to 1; this is the proportion which the total world production of silver bears ta that of gold. Over long periods, taking the amount of gold that has been produced in the world each year in comparison with the amount of silver produced, the ratio has been all the way from 10 to 18 per cent; but over an average of years the output of silver has had a ratio to gold of 16 to 1. That explains why rulers in days gone by adopted that ratio, and that is where we have got it.

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Reid
Canada produces a considerable amount of silver, and in passing I might give the figures for 1932-33. In 1932 we produced 18,347,907 ounces and last year we produced 15,360,764 ounces; and it is carefully estimated that 66 per cent of the silver produced in Canada comes from copper, lead and zinc. Now, regarding the ordinary consumption, if one can use that word with respect to silver, that has also been carefully compiled by those who have given the subject consideration, and it is found that the consumption of silver by various countries has averaged between 200 million and 250 million ounces. But what has brought about the flood of silver during the past few years has been the fact that many countries have not only debased their coinage but have sold the resulting fine silver in the world's markets, thereby bringing down the price. Not only has the throwing of this silver on the market had its effect on price, but there was also the fact that governments were persisting in this practice, and there was no telling how long they would continue to do so. That also had its effect on the price. With respect to the debasement of coinage, it has been estimated by some authorities that Great Britain alone, in ten years, had thrown upon the world's markets 541 million ounces of fine silver-silver taken from her coinage, not silver bought from mines.
During the past number of years, it may interest the house to know, and especially since 1920, there has been an average amount of 200 million ounces of silver thrown on the markets of the world by various countries, all the result of the melting-up of silver coinage. That, on top of world mine production, has demoralized the whole industry and, as I have stated, brought down the price of silver to the lowest point it has been in many years.
Another argument in regard to silver has been that the silver mines would benefit. One man said to me, "You must be boosting for the silver mines." I said to him, "My friend, you have not said anything about the gold mines, though they have had a little Klon-dyke to themselves this past year; for during 1933 they received over $23,000,000 extra for the gold they produced." I am speaking of course of gold produced in Canada. I commented on this not many days ago, and I repeat to-day, that the government should have taken this profit instead of allowing the mine owners to get away with $23,000,000 extra, because I have figures to show that some mines in Canada are producing gold around $15 an ounce, and with the price of gold at $20.67 they were making a fair return on their investment. But when gold went 74726-60
up to $34 and they were allowed to ship it out of this country at that figure they made fabulous fortunes out of gold in one year's transactions. As I have stated, the figures given by the department show the extra money obtained as some $23,380,000. Those profits I believe, during these times especially, should have gone into the exchequer of this country. Others argue that metals are useless. I realize that the ideal system would be one in which the unit of value would remain constant, that a dollar to-day would have the same purchasing value as five or ten years hence. That is something that has been sought for many centuries, but has not yet been attained. I realize also that paper money is not sound money. People still have confidence in metallic coinage. I believe it was the Prime Minister who pointed out in a speech here last year that until the majority of people of the world would confidently accept paper money from other nations, the precious metals, especially gold, if not silver, will have to be used. But one must realize that sixty per cent of the population of the world, 1,600,000,000 people, still use silver; in countries like China, where few banks exist and there it little or no paper money in circulation, every money transaction is carried out with silver or metallic coinage. In India, with its teeming millions, where wealth is reckoned in silver, where dowries given on the marriage of daughters are paid in silver, where money is hoarded as the wealth of the people whether silver is dear or cheap, the accumulated hoards of the people are in the form of silver the value of which is greatly affected by changing values. I am not dealing with a theory; if I were I would probably advocate doing away with all metallic backing for currency, but I realize, as most hon. members do, that most civilized countries-I will not say all civilized, but countries like Great Britain, the United Sates and our own-have built up a monetary system whereby paper has become the instrument of transactions, and in effect the money of the nation.
A change in currency values affects the lives of all, but this power is not held by the government to-day, the money changers own and control the yardstick and can contract or stretch it as they see fit, making the changes to suit themselves, and so in large measure they control the economic life of the people. It has been the bankers and financiers of the world who have forced all countries on to the single standard of gold. As I will endeavour to show, they robbed over 1,600,000,000 people when they forced them to use gold alone as the yardstick or measure of value. Take for instance China; in 1929 the tael was worth.
Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Reid

I believe, 64 cents. To-day it is only worth 34 cents in gold, because the bankers say; We do not want your silver, we are all on the gold standard now-or they said so until recently. So the value of China's silver coinage fell, with the result that China and countries on the silver standard were able to buy much less, as they had to put up so much more silver to buy from countries on the gold standard.
The other night I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question regarding wheat going to China from Australia. I believe the reason Australia has done this greater business in wheat with China is not that Australian wheat is any better than ours for the purposes of the Chinese, but it is due entirely to the exchange factor. Australian currency has a lower exchange value than ours. I will place on Hansard some figures in support of that contention, just giving round figures. In 1929 we imported from Australia over $3,000,000 worth of goods. In 1933 we were importing a little more; it had gone up to over $5,000,000, but our exports to Australia in 1929 were over $19,000,000, whereas last year they had dropped to just a little over $10,000,000 worth. Take Canada's trade with China and see how the figures compare. In 1929 we imported from China almost $3,000,000 worth of goods. In 1933 we were importing a little less, but the startling figures are those in regard to our exports to China. In 1929 they were over $27,000,000, whereas last year we exported to that country only a trifle over $6,500,000. Looking at Australia's trade with China you find that it has greatly increased in the last few years, due to the fact that the currency of Australia was lower even than that of the old country, and also the fact that China, being on a silver basis, could therefore purchase more in Australia than she could in Canada.
One striking fact that I think should be placed on record is that our loss of trade with China is not entirely due to poverty there, as in the case of our own countries, for internally there has been an industrial boom in China during the past three years. The loss of trade between Canada and China has been due not to the poverty of the Chinese but to the fact that we in this country have refused to accept their standard of value, which is silver, and are demanding that they use ours, namely gold.
There are one or two authorities that I would like to quote in support of this resolution, or the idea that countries should adopt silver as a currency basis. The first is Sir George Paish, the distinguished English

economist, who in his recent very interesting and very illuminating book, The Way to Recovery, says:
In considering the possibilities of trade development in China, one has to realize that one is dealing with the second largest country in the world with an area of four millions of square miles and with a population of no less than four hundred millions of soids (approximately one-fifth of the world's entire population) which is considerably greater than India's, two and' a half times greater than Russia's and nearly three and a half times greater than America's. This immense population at present is supplied with less than 8,000 miles of railway and with very few good roads suitable for motor traffic. Were China to build the 100,000 miles of railway contemplated and designed by Sun Yat Sen. and were she to be assisted to accomplish this work in the not distant future by means of loans supplied from abroad, a great stimulus would be given, both to Chinese trade and to the trade of all countries.
As my time is short I shall have to shorten the quotation; I want to get to his last remark:
Furthermore, more active trade in China and the influx of large amounts of foreign capital for many years would' necessitate a much greater supply of silver currency, and by raising the price of silver would enhance the value of China's present immense stock of silver taels. In this way there would be created a renewed spirit of confidence in China and her obligations could be met with much greater ease than is now possible with the price of silver and the value of the tael at the present abnormally and disastrously low levels.
Again take Mr. Kann's report-I haven't time to read it all, but he states in his report of last year:
The sale by governments had a doubly harmful consequence: first, because large extra quantities of silver were thrown on the market, irrespective of whether, when and where these were wanted; and second, the baneful psychological effect caused by the uncertainty, or rather the certainty, of more coming, in the near future. This has been a huge black cloud overshadowing the silver market like the angel of death.
Then I have another authority, Mr. Montagu Norman, governor, and Sir Charles Addis, a member of the board, of the Bank of England, and certainly among the greatest authorities in the world to-day on currency questions, who in their joint report following an inquiry authorized by the British government in 1931, said:
I think that one has to bear in mind the interaction between gold and silver prices. There is a reaction upon gold when an extreme fall or rise takes place in the value of silver, which is none the less serious, because it is indirect and not very apparent on the surface. The consequential changes in the price generally and in trade conditions which would be produced, the disturbance to the world's peace

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Reid
and confidence, the interference with the long established social habits of the people of India in the use of silver, the shock to the reliance of a great country like China upon silver as a medium of currency and a common store of value could' not fail to have important effects upon the gold prices of countries in Europe and, indeed, in America.
Then we had the British economic mission to the far east appointed March 18, 1930, to inquire into the present condition of British trade with China and Japan and to report what action should be taken to develop and increase that trade. Mr. Ernest Thompson was appointed chairman of the mission, which left London in September, 1930, and returned in April of 1931. During that time they made an exhaustive investigation of the trade situation in both Japan and China at a cost of some $300,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION PROPOSING ISSUANCE OP PAPER MONEY AGAINST SILVER AT FIXED RATIO TO GOLD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope my hon. friend will appreciate that naturally I desire to conclude anything I have to say before six o'clock rather than to break it into two parts. I hope he realizes that while I should like to extend him the courtesy of a longer period, he has had six minutes additional, and in the circumstances perhaps he will not object.
In the second recital of his resolution the hon. member states:
And whereas for centuries past, silver was the only precious metal used, both as currency and as the unit of value for the interchange of goods and services.
I call the attention of the house to the expression "for centuries past, silver was the only precious metal used." In that statement

he has hardly conformed to the past, because as a matter of fact gold coins were in existence in the days of the ancient Greeks and Romans; in the year 1660 there was gold coinage in Great Britain, and there has been gold coinage from that time down to the present. It is true that prior to that for a period, particularly in the dark ages, silver was the predominant metal, but dating from the year 1660 gold was in the ascendant, until at the beginning of the nineteenth century it had entirely excluded silver as a basis of the monetary standard, and left it to be used as subsidiary coinage. That condition obtained down to the period when, for reasons which one need not discuss at this time, Great Britain in the year 1931 was driven off the gold standard.
In the fourth recital of his resolution the hon. member uses the following expression:
Coupled with the very limited amount of gold available in the world for the interchange of good's and services.
I have no doubt the hon. member has inadvertently fallen into the same error under which so many seem to labour, namely that a shortage of gold was responsible in part at least for the debacle which overtook the worid in the year 1929. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, that statement cannot be substantiated. The most that can be said is that there was a maldistribution of gold, which is an entirely different thing from saying that there was not sufficient gold. In that connection may I point out that the gold delegation of the League of Nations went into this matter very thoroughly in the year 1932, and in the preliminary data prepared for the meeting of that delegation there was some suggestion in keeping with the idea under which the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) seems to be labouring, namely that there is a shortage of world gold. I quote from page 32 of the League of Nations report for the year 1932.
Before proceeding further in our analysis of the problem of gold supply we wish at this point to record our opinion that the world's total stock of monetary gold, apart from any considerations as to its distribution among different countries, has at all times in recent years been adequate to support the credit structure legitimately required by world trade, and that the rapid decline in prices which began in 1929 cannot be attributed to any deficiency in the gold' supply considered in this sense. During the six years from the end of 1925 to the end of 1931 the world's central gold reserves increased from about $9,150,000,000 to about $11,350,000,000, or at an average rate of 3| per cent per annum. Since this rate is not lower than the generally accepted normal rate of growth of production and trade in the

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Rhodes
gold using countries as a whole, and since, in addition, certain economies were made in the use of gold, at any rate in the earlier part of the period considered, there seems to be little ground for believing that the total supplies of gold available for monetary use have not been sufficient to meet all reasonable demands.
In that regard may I point out that I do not think it can be established there was not ample credit in 1929. As a matter of fact I think we may very well argue that one of our difficulties at that time was that there was too much credit, and that being so, that credit was based, so far as gold is a base for credit, upon the then existing supply of gold in the world.
What do we find since that time? In 1930, 20,160,355 ounces of gold were produced which, not at $35 an ounce, but at the old value of $20.67 per ounce, represented an increase in the monetary gold of that year of $416,751,523. In 1931 there was the largest amount of gold produced up to that time in a single year, in the history of the world, so far as history is available on the point. In that year the production was 21,300,000 ounces, at a value of $440,200,000. In 1932 there was a still further increase to 24,163,000 ounces of gold, at a value of $499,444,000. In 1933, on an estimated figure,, the amount of production was 24,282,000 ounces, at a total value of $501,908,940, or a total production in those four years of $1,858,309,463, and these figures represent a yearly increase in the world's gold supply at a percentage greater than was ever known before. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MOTION PROPOSING ISSUANCE OP PAPER MONEY AGAINST SILVER AT FIXED RATIO TO GOLD
speechtext:
Yes. As a matter of fact, the question asked by the hon. member for Weyburn raises the age old question which gave rise to the maxim that men dig gold in Africa and bury it in India, because as a
matter of fact down through the centuries, until England went off the gold standard in 1931, that very condition did obtain, and millions upon millions of dollars worth of gold were poured into India to remain there, some to be buried, some to go into the form of ornaments and some to be used in the arts. But, as a matter of fact, that flow into India ceased. In fact, in September 1931 there was an outflow, with the result that the bullion brokers in London estimate that from September, 1931, to the end of 1933 approximately $565,000,000 worth of gold has come out of India. That is the valuation placed upon the basis of $20.67 per ounce and not upon the world price.
So far as the value of gold is concerned I might make reference to the fact that wholesale prices are in a far different status from what they were in 1929. Although I do not think for the purpose of my argument it is necessary to enter into that matter, it is interesting to note, taking the year 1913 as an average of one hundred, that in the year 1929 wholesale prices stood at 135; in 1930 at 114; in 1931; at 92; in 1932 at 81; in 1933 at 81. So it will be seen that while there is not an absolute equation between the value of gold and commodity price?, because the reserves against bank deposits and liabilities have a bearing on the case so that the ratio will not be exact, nevertheless it is certainly fair to say that a given amount of gold will go much further in the purchase of commodities on the lower commodity price scale.
So I would say this, that not only has there been a normal world increase in the supply of gold, but a greatly accelerated increase, and there are four factors which should be considered by my hon. friend from New Westminster in regard to the amount of gold in the world. First, there is the question of increased production. Second, there is the return for currency use of gold hitherto hoarded or stored away in India. Third, there is the question of the revaluation of gold, which has had the effect so far as the United States is concerned, when it increased the price of gold from $20.67 to $35 per ounce, of increasing its value by nearly 70 per cent, or, to be exact, 69-3 per cent. Fourth, there is the factor that while hitherto the accepted amount of gold as an appropriate basis for currency has been in the neighbourhood of 40 per cent, it will be within the recollection of the house that at the recent world monetary and economic conference it was agreed that 25 per cent would be sufficient. Upon that point perhaps I should read from the appendix to the report of the world monetary and economic confer-

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Rhodes
ence, where at page 13 are set out the resolutions that were adopted, and I find these:
(c)	That under modern conditions monetary gold is required not for internal circulation but as a reserve against central bank liabilities and primarily to meet external demands for payments caused by some disequilibrium on the foreign account. It is consequently undesirable to put gold coins or gold certificates into internal circulation.
(d)	That in order to improve the working of a future gold standard greater elasticity should be given to central bank legal cover provisions; for instance, in so far as the system of percentage gold cover is applied a minimum ratio of not more than twenty-five per cent should be considered as sufficient; similar elasticity should be achieved by appropriate measures where other systems are applied. However, such changes must not be taken as an excuse for unduly building up a larger superstructure of notes and credits; in other words, the effect of this resolution should be to increase the free reserve of central banks and thereby to strengthen their position.
My hon. friend at the outset of his remarks said that his resolution was not put forward as suggesting a panacea. To quote his exact words, which I took down at the time, he said that the effect of his resolution, if adopted, would go a long way towards stabilization, or at least it would be a step in that direction. May I say to my hon. friend, with all deference, that the effect of this resolution, if it could be put into effect, would be precisely the opposite, and I will give the reasons why in my judgment that is so.
In his resolution my hon. friend calls for silver to have a fixed ratio to gold. Now assume that we did that. We would have to fix the ratio-a difficult thing at best, but suppose we used our best judgment in respect
to it. This is what would happen. If we fixed the ratio to gold at a point where silver became higher than its present market value we would then have silver flowing to this country from the four corners of the earth, and the principle of Gresham's law would apply. The result would be that our gold would disappear and we would in effect find ourselves on a silver basis, which I think even my hon. friend from New Westminster will agree would be a very unstable basis; for whatever may be said of the respective merits of gold and silver, the fact remains that gold has been far more constant, and in the very nature of things must be far more constant, in its value than silver.
Now let us put the argument the other way. Let us assume that we put the price of silver at a lower figure than its present market price. In that event we would get no silver. We would then be confined to one metal base, and that would be gold.
Again, you might say fix the ratio of silver to gold upon a basis which represents the metallic value of silver to-day. But then what would happen? We would have fluctuations in the price of the metal. If a new mine were discovered and silver became cheap we would have disequilibrium at once. While on that point let me indicate that from the period 1866 to 1885 the average market ratio of gold to silver was 17 to 1. My ho-n. friend in the course of his remarks quoted the ratio 16 to 1, but as a matter of fact from 1866 down to the present time there has not been anything approaching a ratio of 16 to 1. I am taking it at its lowest point from a list of the percentages during past years which I shall now give:

Let me make it clear at once that I quite sympathize with my hon. friend from New Westminster in the object he has in mind in moving this resolution, but as I have already indicated, if we attempted to fix our currency on a fixed ratio of silver to gold the effect would be to make foT disequilibrium, not for stabilization. In other words, it would have the very opposite effect to that my hon. friend desires.

I do not propose'-I would not, even if I felt myself the most competent authority in the world-to enter into an argument in principle as to whether there should or should not be bimetallism, whether we should have our currency based on a fixed ratio of silver to gold. But for the purposes of this discussion we do not need to enter into that phase of the subject at all. Let us, for the purposes of discussion, admit that that is the ideal

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Rhodes
situation. I make mention of that for this reason: If we are to have bimetallism, its only chance of survival is through international agreement. As I have pointed out, otherwise there would be a flow of gold and silver back and forth to the absolute confusion of currencies.
I made note of one or two remarks by the hon. member which show how easily we can be led astray even with the best of intentions. I understand that my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), who has made a great study of this important subject, will refer more particularly to the trade features. I must say that I got some mild amusement from the arguments used by the hon. member with respect to the trade with China. He referred to the fact that because silver was cheap, in order to purchase goods from a gold country the Chinaman had to use more silver. Strange as it may appear, the argument is just the other way. China never purchases goods with silver; she purchases silver with goods. Down through all the years China has been an importer of silver. The fact of the matter is that the cheaper silver is, the less goods it takes to buy it. Possibly this may have something to do with the remarks of my hon. friend concerning the great industrial boom in China. I have no doubt my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce will refer to this at greater length.
The hon. member referred to the silver dollar. I am speaking from memory but I think it is since 1916 that we have had upon our statute books legislation to enable us to mint a silver dollar. Possibly the circumstance that we have allowed that statute to remain unused for some eighteen years is an indication that perhaps the people of this country do not want to carry around a cumbersome silver dollar or, as it is known colloquially in the United States, a cart-wheel. I have an open mind upon the subject and I am sure that no one would be more delighted than this government if the people of this country deemed it wise to take kindly to silver dollars. On that point we have an absolutely open mind and it is a fair subject for discussion. Possibly it might be discussed in the committee on banking and commerce. What holds good with respect to silver dollars, holds equally good with respect to silver certificates which would be covered by an equal metal coverage.
The hon. member commended us for the silver agreement arrived at at the monetary and economic conference, but he said that we should have gone further. May I point
out to the hon. member for New Westminster and to the house that some forty-six nations of the world sat around the table and studied closely this matter. This agreement represents in cold type the maximum distance which they felt they could go. The hon. member referred to certain provisions of this agreement. Provision (c) reads:
That they shall substitute silver coins for low-value paper currency in so far as the budgetary and local conditions of each country will permit.
That provision has no reference to Canada but it does refer to the inordinate use of small denomination paper currency by many continental countries. I may say to my hon. friend that that provision, harmless as it may seem, was the result of a great deal of discussion and it was regarded as a real concession on the part of those countries that they should be prepared to substitute silver coins for their notes of small denomination.
The hon. member referred to what he regarded as the disparity in the proportionate amount of silver which Canada must produce as the result of being a party to the London agreement. Let me poiint out to him that that agreement provides for the removal from the world's markets over a period of four years of 35,000,000 ounces of silver per year. The proportion as allocated to Canada has no reference to-day to its proper proportion as a silver producer of the total amount of
35,000,000 ounces, but it did more nearly when the agreement was originally drafted. There were one or two smaller countries, whose names I need not mention, who were expected to become parties to the agreement, but they did not do so. For reasons which I need not discuss here, the United States, being very anxious that this silver agreement should go through, agreed to add the share which these countries failed to take up to their own share. Barring that contingency, the original setup provided for the purchase on the part of Canada of 1,671,802 fine ounces of silver. That amount represented our fair proportion as a producing country oif silver over a period of years. Under these circumstances I submit that no fault oan properly be found for our not having fallen into the terms and spirit of the agreement. I may say to my hon. friend that no exception was taken; on the contrary, the signatories to the agreement were eminently satisfied with the amount which Canada agreed to take.

subtopic: MOTION PROPOSING ISSUANCE OP PAPER MONEY AGAINST SILVER AT FIXED RATIO TO GOLD
speechtext:
Before the amendment is
put I should like to say a few words. I was hoping some hon. members might have given expression to their views on this important matter.
The amendment is a simple one; it suggests that, inasmuch as certain steps were taken and certain decisions arrived at at the world econ-

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Stevens
omic conference, the house recognize what was done at that conference and endorse the action of the delegates from Canada. I think this is a perfectly sound thing to do. The matter is in a sense of a dual nature; there is the academic side, simply a general study in economics, and there is the other phase, the practical or administrative aspect. I am speaking now of the general question of bimetallism, if you like, or the remonetization of silver, or the problem of currency generally. In the amendment we do not pass judgment one way or the other on the academic question, but welcome measures that were taken at the world economic conference as at least a practical step in the right direction. It is with that view that I have seconded the amendment and given support to the views of my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes).
I should like, however, to take the opportunity of saying a few words on the question in a general way. As I said a moment ago, it divides itself naturally into two sections, the academic and the practical or administrative. The success of the latter depends upon the acceptance of the former in a world wide sense. In other words it is not much use in Canada taking steps for the remonetization of silver unless there is some acceptance of the policy by other influential countries. I would not say that all countries must fall into line, but certainly one must recognize that the leaders in exchange and in control of international monetary affairs are perhaps three countries, Great Britain, the United States and France-London, New York and Paris. One of course can add other European countries having tremendous influence, such as Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and so on, but the three great centres I have mentioned have long been recognized as the dominating centres of international exchange. So if those countries at least are not adopting an international exchange policy similar to that proposed by any resolution we may adopt, obviously we could have little success with it. Recognition of that situation caused me to realize long ago that, attractive though bimetallism-and I use the term in its broad general sense-may be, it is impractical and useless for Canada to attempt it alone. But inasmuch as the subject has been brought before parliament, perhaps I may take a short time to discuss the problem from an academic or an economic standpoint. No harm can be done by that, and certainly I welcome the opportunity.
My hon. friend the member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), who introduced the resolution, brings it forward at this time in
perfect good faith, I have no doubt; but some of us who brought the question up three, four, or five years ago received little support then; until last year very little interest was evidenced in the matter by others in the house or out of it. During the last year it became a much more popular idea and therefore of course attractive from the point of view of its being a matter for discussion in the House of Commons. Perhaps if we had been giving more attention to it during the years of the depression we might have been able to observe a larger measure of progress at this time than we do find in this or other countries. Statesmen throughout the world, during the past four years particularly, have been looking for some measure for stabilizing prices, something that would be satisfactory to all countries. They have also been looking for a better foundation for currency, because it must be admitted that the basis of currency in many countries has been sadly dislocated; there has been loss of confidence not only in the currency of some countries but in the credit of the countries themselves. World statesmen and economists of note have been looking for these stabilizing factors, for some measure acceptable to all for the control of international exchange. But nothing has been found that is generally acceptable to the nations of the world.
A few of us-speaking in a general sense- in different countries have held the view that had silver been joined with gold it would have formed a suitable background for currency; that it would have led to the stabilizing of international exchange and a wider degree of confidence in the currencies of the world, and perhaps would have materially helped towards the stabilizing of prices. That is a view that has been held by many. However, as I have intimated, it has not found acceptance among the nations of the world. It may be recalled that in 1921 John Maynard Keynes, one of the most widely known economists

I suppose one can scarcely say that any one economist is an authority, but certainly Mr. Keynes is widely known-suggested that wheat or butter or iron might be used as a basis for currency. Then another school of thought held the view that currency should be issued against commodities produced, the currency being retired as the commodities went into consumption. But in respect of all these suggestions, and they have been numerous, it immediately became clear that currency resting upon such a basis would be as variable as the quantity of the product upon which it was founded. For instance, Keynes for some time rather emphasized wheat, a commodity of world-wide use, as a

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Stevens
stable basis for currency, but when in 1928 nearly the whole world had a bumper crop and there was a huge surplus of wheat on the markets of the world, he realized then if not before that currency based upon a commodity of that kind would be extremely variable in its character. So these suggestions have not met with favour. But they are indications that thinkers the world over have been trying to find some way in which the currencies of the world might be more firmly founded upon some basis commonly acceptable to all.
Now I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, referring to the subject in a general way and discussing it, shall I say, from an academic standpoint. Silver, as the hon. member who introduced the resolution said, has been used as a background for currency from time immemorial. It might be well to remember that it served in a very satisfactory way all through the centuries until it was demonetized by legislative action in the last century; I think 1873 was the main year of departure. In other words, silver was recognized as a sound and safe background for currency, being used in some countries in conjunction with gold but in most countries as the sole background until it was demonetized. Demonetization of silver took the form of simply closing the mints of the world to silver, and I refer to that for this reason: there are many who contend that because silver has fallen in value, that is evidence that it has no higher value, but the reason silver has fallen to the exent it has in recent years is that it lost its power or its usefulness as money or currency and became a commodity like tin, zinc, lead or iron, and now silver is a commodity and only a commodity. Previously it was a money faotor and was also used in the arts and sciences, but having been denied entry to the mints as a material out of which money was made, it lost that value and became merely an ordinary commodity on the market, and of course it fell in Value.
An interesting thing to note, Mr. Speaker, is the historic ratio of silver, to which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) referred this afternoon, as did the hon. member who introduced the resolution. There was a consistency about the ratio of silver to gold as long as it was used as a currency which is rather striking and, to my mind, a bit startling. In the Roman period it was twelve to one and stood at that ratio for many years, in fact for many centuries, I think. Then for several centuries France and England had it fixed by law at fifteen and a half to one. and I think this ratio was accepted by the Stevens.]
United States as well as by the Latin union, that is, France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, if I remember rightly. This ratio obtained for several hundred years. It is interesting also to note that for a period of at least one hundred years prior to 1873 silver did not vary in value more than one point; the variation was very slight indeed. As as matter of fact in 1717 an investigation was conducted by Sir Isaac Newton and a very interesting report on this subject which can be found in the library here, was made to the British government. Sir Isaac Newton confirmed the ratio of fifteen and a half to one and, as I say. that ratio obtained during the centuries with apparent satisfaction.
We have had figures given to-day in regard to the production of silver. I have a few figures that are slightly different, but they largely confirm what has been stated previously. In a period of approximately four hundred years, from 1493 to 1931, there have been produced about 14,500,000,000 ounces of silver. I am referring to this because I think it is importamt to keep in mind the question of the production of silver. There is a fear in the minds of some that the production of silver would increase so rapidly as literally to swamp the market should silver be remonetized. The ratio of production, as I have already intimated, has been about fourteen and a half to one over a period of five hundred years. In the last fifty years, however, the ratio has been about 14-4 to one. The latter figure is accurate; the former figure is accepted the world over as a fair figure. But the significant point is that eighty per cent of the world's silver is produced as a byproduct, and I think this constitutes a safeguard to the overproduction of silver. For instance, if there was a tendency to speed up the production of silver to an unwarranted degree it would result in an increased production of lead, zinc and copper, the three metals with which silver is usually associated, to an extent that would constitute a great overproduction of these other metals and result in a disastrous drop in the prices of such metals. So where there might be a tendency to increase the production of silver unduly there would be that natural brake in the tendency to reduce the production of these other commodities. I do not share the view at all that necessarily there would be an overproduction of silver. The sources of supply are well known; in 1930 Mexico produced 105,000,000 ounces, the United States,
49,000,000 ounces, Canada, 26,000,000 ounces, South America, 25,000,000 ounces, and miscellaneous countries, 35,000,000 ounces.

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Stevens

speechtext:
No, I think not. My
own view is that there is not a likelihood of any overproduction. Mexico, of course, is overwhelmingly the greatest producer of silver.
I do not think there is any danger of overproduction in Canada or the United States.
Now I should like to say just a word as to the use of silver in the arts and industries, which must not be lost sight of. About thirty-five per cent of the silver produced is used in the arts and industries. For instance, the United States uses 25,000,000 ounces annually; the United Kingdom uses 6,000,000 ounces, and the miscellaneous other countries use about 20,000,000 ounces.
Then there is the question of the market for silver. As the Minister of Finance very properly pointed out this, afternoon, India and China have been the great consuming markets for silver; they are importers to a very large extent. As a matter of fact, in 1929 China and India between them imported about 220,000,000 ounces of silver. In 1932, however, they imported much less, China about 80,000,000 ounces and India about 12,000,000 ounces. No doubt this falling off was due to the drop in the price of silver in the world market and also to the adoption in India of the definite gold policy and the offering for sale of large quantities of silver. For instance, as a result of going on the gold standard in 1925, I think, India had about 300,000,000 ounces of silver placed in the treasury which they felt they had to feed out to the market. That was over and above the requirements of the country for coinage, and in a few years about 90,000,000 ounces were sold. It was the sale of this large amount of silver, plus the debasing of the ooinage of Europe, that really created the catastrophe to the silver market of the world. For instance France, by turning to aluminum, to paper francs and so on, released 60,000,000 ounces of silver in the six or eight years between 1924 and 1930 or thereabouts, and India released 300,000,000 ounces. Then in Great Britain, where coinage was debased from -925 fine to -500, they released some 82,000,000 ounces. This gives an indication of the amount of silver which came on to the market, not from production, but from the abandonment of a high standard of silver in coinage, and in the case of India the abandonment of the silver basis for all its coinage and the adoption of the gold standard. It is estimated that as a result of the debasing of the silver coinage of the world during a ten year period 408,000,000 ounces were released on the markets of the world. That is one of the reasons why I
consider that the international conference of last summer in its agreement regarding silver did something that was very useful in this connection, because it bound certain countries to cease the debasing of currency and as early as possible to restore the high standard; and, on the other hand, it provided that certain producing countries should absorb a portion of their production within their own boundaries.
For instance, Belgium has already issued a new silver coinage. One of the first coins minted I received the other day from the International Chamber of Commerce. They have restored a -825 fine standard. That is a practical and useful contribution to the solution of the silver problem of the world.
