I wish now to turn briefly to a reference to China made by the hon. member. If he will permit me to say so, the mistake he made in referring to Chinese or oriental trade and its relation to silver is this:	The business of China, as we understand it, is done largely at Shanghai; it is centred at Shanghai. At that point you have the great banks of China, and may I say there are some very powerful banking institutions. [DOT] In Shanghai there are located to a large degree the industrial and commercial activities of northern China. Of course, Canton in the south is the other great centre. But while it is true in the back country of China silver is still used as the currency, and while in those parts they prefer to have silver in some form, yet in the Shanghai centre the bankers are against the readoption of silver as the background for currency in other countries of the world, because, as the Minister of Finance quite properly pointed out, it would mean the raising of the price of silver, and therefore they would have to ship out more goods for the same quantity of silver. They take the position that the low silver market is helpful to the dealer in goods manufactured or otherwise in the exporting centre of Shanghai, and so they are opposed to the remonetiza-

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Stevens
tion of silver. On the other hand may I give my own opinion, for what it is worth. I am of the view that if silver were remonetized and raised in value so that in the older trading countries of the world it would have a higher purchasing value, the people in the back country of China, those parts away from the trading centres of Shanghai and Canton, would experience an increased purchasing power and there would be a stimulus to trade. However, there is a distinct cleavage of opinion on that point. There are those who argue strongly that it is much better that silver should be low so that dealers in goods, and manufacturers, exporters and importers in the great centres of Canton and Shanghai can get silver as cheaply as possible, rather than have it at a higher price to increase purchasing power in the country behind.
Furthermore, it is interesting to note in regard to China that Shanghai is one of the few plaices, if not the only one, in the wodd where gold as sold purely as a commodity. In the great royal gold exchange in Shanghai they have a huge building devoted to this purpose alone, where gold is traded in every day just the same as in this country wheat is traded at Winnipeg, or as in the United States corn is traded in Chicago or the metals in New York.

speechtext:
It is in bars, the exact
weight of which I have not in mind. Each bar consists of a certain number of ounces, but I shall not risk saying what size they are. However it is a certain gold bar, stamped by the Chinese authorities, and traded in the royal gold exchange just the same as other commodities are traded in exchanges. That is a most interesting point. Furthermore it is mot correct to assume that in China there is no understanding of a gold currency, because in that country gold has been used as a currency for some five thousand years. If any hon. member wishes to study the matter he will find in the library a very interesting work on the subject written by a gentleman whose name for the moment escapes me, but who is one of the most outstanding authorities. The book was only recently published and is most interesting reading. I make this reference only because it is well to have the facte before us when we are dealing with these subjects. The question, therefore, of the trade with China does not enter into the matter in quite as aggravated a form as at first it would appear, but it is possible, quite possible-and I do not wish too strongly to contradict the

hon. member who introduced the resolution- it is quite possible if, and I must use capital letters for that word, "if" silver were readopted by the leading nations of the world, that ultimately it would be a benefit to those people living in the oriental countries and away from the great centres to which I have referred.
A word more regarding the position silver has held for centuries in the trading markets of the world. I have intimated there was not very much variation in its price until the year 1873. As indicated by the Minister of Finance, from 1873 onward there has been a constant fluctuation in the prioe of silver, but there is a very definite and distinct reason for that. Up to 1873 silver was recognized in all the great trading nations of the world as a monetary medium. The mimte of these counteies were open to silver. Then, following the Franco-German war and the acquisition by Germany of huge quantities of gold, Germany closed her mints to silver, and 'Great Britam, which had been following a bimetallic system from 1816 onward under which gold and silver were both recognized, closed its mrnte to silver. Shortly afterwards France-and the Latin union were forced to close their mints to silver, and then the price of silver fell off very rapidly.
The Minister of Finance gave prices in percentages, but I have here some prices which

hwT-'i In ~1S83 ifc had fallen to ShH; in 1898 it was 78 cents; in 1894, 60 cents, and it
remained , 'at 60 or 55 cents or thereabouts until the great war. During the great war there was a veiy large demand for silver to pay for the goods taken from the orient, and silver rose to $1.30 and, at one time I think, to $1.80 an ounce. But immediately after the war the price fell again to $1.01 in 1920, land in 1930 the lowest price was 26 cents. The decline' over that long period' of years carried silver down to 50 cents, where it remained for a number of years, and then it fell subsequent to the depression to as low as 26 cents. The fluctuation in the price of silver after 1873 was due to the closing of the mints to silver. If anyone is interested in getting a view of that particulfar period when the mints of Great Britain and Germany, and later of France, were closed to silver, they will find in the debates of the British House-

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Young
of Commons of 1889 a debate on a resolution introduced by Mr. W. H. Smith, of Yorkshire.
I <am speaking from memory but I think I have the facts correctly. Mr. Smith introduced a resolution indicating that by 1889 there had resulted such an interference with trade because of the demonetization of silver that it threatened the welfare of the nation, or something to that effect. Sir Edward Go sehen was Chancellor of the Exchequer at the time and he took part in the debate. I remember reading his argument, and in a word, it was this: To interfere in 1889, the time :at which he was speaking, with the decision of 1873 would result An such a dislocation of financial arrangements in the money market of London that he did not contemplate the results with equanimity. In his speeich however he expressed a degree of acquiescence in the views of Mr. Smith, and the most interesting feature of all of that debate was an address by the late Lord Balfour, then Mr. Arthur Balfour. He was then a young man and on that occasion he made a speech which would repay the time given to a reading of it because in it he indicated What in his opinion would be the ultimate effect of this demonetization of silver in the leading countries of the world. If you will read his utterances of that day, in 1889, in the light of what has happened since, you can only conclude that he had a prophetic vision. I may say that Mr. Balfour, afterwards Lord Balfour, held that opinion to the day of his death, because only a few months before he died he gave expression to a similar view.
But the point that we are concerned with at the present moment is not the theory of bimetallism, which I frankly state to the house is one that I hold,, bimetallism constituting a suitable backing for international currency if acceptable to the leading countries of the world; but we are dealing to-night with what this country and this government should do. I should like to see this country in a position where it could again accept silver into its mints as freely as gold. I Should like to see the larger 'countries of the world do it; but the world thinks differently. The world monetary and economic conference of last summer went into this matter with great care and came to the decision which we have before us as a parliament.
I submit to the house that whatever may be the view we as individuals may have on the theory of this subject is not necessarily the view which we should ask parliament to act upon, but rather we should act in conformity with the most progressive steps taken by the leading countries of the world, and
that we have before us in the form of the agreement to which reference has been made by the Minister of Finance to-day. It is for that reason, recognizing that we can only go as far as it is practicable for us to go, that I have seconded the minister's amendment, Which virtually declares that this house accepts the decision so taken, not necessarily as indicating final action or the final step, but being for the moment all that we can practically do towards the restoration of silver to its old position as copartner with gold as a backing for the currency of the world.

subtopic: MOTION PROPOSING ISSUANCE OP PAPER MONEY AGAINST SILVER AT FIXED RATIO TO GOLD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, both the resolution and the amendment are in my opinion based on the belief so commonly held in these days that you can increase the wealth of the world in some way or other by juggling with the yardstick by which it is measured. We are told that the present depression came upon us because of an artificial increase in the value of gold. Gold is the standard of value of the western countries. Silver is the standard of value of the eastern countries. We are told that by artificially increasing our standard of value disaster has been brought upon the western world; then we are asked by the same persons to do the very same thing with the standard of value of the eastern countries. We are asked to do with silver what was done with gold. Would not the same results follow? If artificially increasing the value of gold brought disaster to us, would not artificially increasing the value of silver, the standard of China, bring disaster to China? China produces no silver; she buys her silver. Does China buy silver with goods or goods with silver? If she buys goods with silver and we artificially increase the price of silver, then when we sell wheat to China we shall have to give her more wheat for the same quantity of silver; in other words, we shall have to accept a lower price for our wheat. If, on the other hand, China buys silver with goods, and you artificially increase the price of silver, you compel China to pay more for the silver she requires. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) had a very clear understanding of this when he spoke this afternoon. I took down his words. He said "China never purchases goods with silver; she purchases silver with goods. Down through all the years China has been an importer of silver. The fact of the matter is that the cheaper silver is, the less goods it takes to buy it. This may have something to do with the remarks of my hon. friend concerning the great industrial boom in China." In other

Bimetallic Currency-Mr. Young
words, China is prosperous because silver is of low value. The Minister of Finance showed a clear understanding of the matter when he uttered those words. Then I take the agreement that he signed as Minister of Finance at the world monetary and economic conference, in which I find this:
Whereas, it is to the advantage of China that sales from monetary stocks of silver be offset by purchases as herein provided, with a view to its effective stabilization,
And so on. In other words, the Minister of Finance proved in his speech this afternoon that a low price for silver was an advantage to China, and then he asks us to support an agreement that seeks to bring back prosperity to China by artificially increasing the price of silver. The minister this afternoon made a conclusive answer, an unanswerable answer, to the agreement which he himself signed as minister.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) told us a few moments ago that the big bankers and business men of Shanghai and other seaports of China are opposed to the remonetization of silver. But, he said, when you go into the interior where silver is still the only medium of exchange, to artificially increase the price of silver would increase the purchasing power of the people who live there. A Chinaman with an ounce of silver in his possession, if you suddenly doubled the value of silver, would undoubtedly have his purchasing power increased, but how long would that increased purchasing power last? It would last for only one transaction. The Chinaman with an ounce of silver which he has earned goes into a store, and if you have doubled the value of silver by some such measure as this he can buy twice as much of the things he needs, but then in order to get his next ounce of silver he will have to give twice as much labour or twice as much of the goods he has to sell. So this increased purchasing power that would go to the Chinaman would last only one day.
The Minister of Finance proved conclusively this afternoon that there was sufficient gold in the world to serve as a standard for all monetary purposes. Why then should we go out of our way and pledge this and all other governments to buy silver at more than its value and take it off the market? There is no necessity for it, as it is not needed as a standard. The minister has proved this.
It is the most amazing thing of anything that has happened in public life for many years, to find that a small group of men from the different countries that produce silver were able to influence not only their own governments but all governments of the world to

buy their commodity at more than its worth and take it off the market. This applied not only to the countries that were going to benefit, that is, the countries that had silver to sell, but even to China which had silver to buy. I think it is the most amazing thing that ever happened in the history of lobbying. This group of lobbyists were able to convince not only those members who represented mining districts, not only the governments of the countries that produced silver, but the governments of the countries that had to buy silver. These governments were influenced to increase artificially the price of silver, to buy it and take it off the market. For example, they influenced countries like India which had vast quantities of silver to sell; that country needed the money but they were persuaded to hold their silver off the market in order that the silver producers could dig more silver out of the ground and get a good price for it. When we see such phenomena as that, we almost despair of the power of the human race to govern itself.

That is quite a different thing from the Indian people. To-day the Indian people are still valuing their wealth in silver and with the low price of silver at present prevailing they are turning in their paper rupees to purchase bar silver for trading and hoarding. It is not correct to say that the Indians are selling silver; the Indian government is but not the Indian people. They are still large purchasers.

The Minister of Finance spoke about the maladministration of gold. Mr. Winston Churchill has stated that the road back to gold is not going to be easy, in fact it is going to be very difficult. Three countries own practically all the gold supply of the world and it is going to be a difficult matter to redistribute that commodity. An attempt is being made to do this by revaluation.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the Minister of Finance who gave figures with reference to the ratio of gold supply to output. I am afraid he and I will have to agree to differ. The figures which I gave before and which I intend to give now were obtained from what I believe to be an authentic source. They state that from 1906 to the present time gold production has not increased; in fact the production in 1932 was away below
the production in other years between 1906 and 1932. These are the figures given by the bureau of metal statistics and I take them to be fairly authentic.

In conclusion, may I assure the house that I am not pleading for the silver mines alone, and I might say I have no personal interest in them; I am simply interested in the welfare of the people of this country and those engaged in that business. maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
moved: -
That, in the opinion of this house, the question of issuing bilingual state currency, notes and bonds should be referred to a special committee consisting of Messrs. Hackett, Gobeil, Bourgeois, Bell (St. Antoine), Nicholson, Gott, Plunkett, Price, Malcolm, Ralston, Lapointe, Cardin, Casgrain, Rinfret, and Lucas, with power to send for papers, summon witnesses and report from time to time.
Mr. Speaker, the present question is certainly worthy of the consideration of the House. I, therefore, immediately put the following question: Have not Canadian members an interest in placing the problem of 74726-61
bilingual currency on a basis of " bonne entente,'' so as to better study it in the light of what is right and just and so that the French Canadian element would derive some benefit?
The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger), stated, last year, in nicely couched and worthy terms, when he discussed his resolution, that bilingual currency is not a new question to the house. I note, in the debates of this house, that, at the 1906-07 session, the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne), questioned Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, with reference to the stamping of currency and printing of government notes in the two official languages of this country. Mr. Fielding replied that this innovation did not seem to him widely requested. The house will observe that ever since, that date the answer has not varied. You will find the questions and answers at page 6015, volume IV of Hansard, session 1906-07.
I shall not attempt to give an account of the debate which took place on this delicate subject. I am aware that the hon. member for Bellechasse is sincere and I also have no doubt about the sincerity of the seconder; to both I extend my congratulations for their zeal in promoting the success of this cause.
The hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), when the resolution of the hon. member for Bellechasse was discussed, proved beyond all doubt, according to the evidence, that bilingual currency should have its place in this country, by virtue of our rights and after proving that it was so stipulated in our statutes, he added:
Is the principle of bilingual state currency, notes and bonds, a sound principle? My
answer is yes.
What is the status of the French language at the present time? To answer, that question I must go back to 1840. At that time, during the third and fourth years of the reign of Her Majesty Queen Victoria, there was passed an act, which in 3 and 4 Victoria, chapter 35, to reunite the provinces of lower and upper Canada. By this act the French language was prohibited, but this prohibition was lifted on August 14, 1848, by 11 and 12 Victoria, chapter 56. I should like to direct the attention of the house to that chapter. It is entitled:
"An act to repeal so much of an act of the third and fourth years of her present majesty, to reconcile the provinces of upper and lower Canada, and for the government of Canada, as related to the use of the English language in instruments relating to the legislative council and legislative assembly of the provinces of Canada. This is how the statute reads:
Whereas by an act passed in the session of parliament held in the third and fourth years of her present majesty, intituled an act to reunite the provinces of upper and lower Canada, and for the government of Canada, it

962	COMMONS
Bilingual Currency-Mr. Barrette
is amongst other things enacted, that from and after the said reunion of the said two provinces, all writs, proclamations, instruments for summoning and calling together the legislative council ar.d legislative assembly of the province of Canada, and for proroguing and dissolving the same, and all writs of summons and elections-
I should like to direct attention to the following words:
-and all writs and public instruments whatsoever relating to the said legislative council and legislative assembly, or either of them, and all returns to such writs and instruments, and all journals-
I should like to direct particular attention to the next words:
-entries and written or printed proceedings of what nature soever, of the said legislative council and legislative assembly, and of each of them respectively, and all written and printed proceedings and reports of committees of the said legislative council and legislative assembly respectively, shall be in the English language only: Provided always, that the said enactment should not be construed to prevent translated copies of any such documents being made, but no such copy should be kept among the records of the legislative council or legislative assembly, or be deemed in any case to have the force of an original record:
And whereas it is expedient to alter the law in this respect, in order that the legislature of the province of Canada, or the said legislative council and legislative assembly respectively, may have power to make such regulations herein as to them may seem advisable; be it therefore enacted by the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and temporal, and commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, that from and after the passing of this act, so much of the said recited act as is hereinbefore recited shall be repealed."
In constitutional law does not the repeal of a prohibition render the thing prohibited permissible, permitted, legal and constitutional? Therefore may 1 not conclude that bilingual currency, having been prohibited by 3 and 4 Victoria, chapter 35, became permissible, permitted, legal and constitutional when 3 and 4 Victoria was repealed?
Among parliamentarians, who, years ago, shone in the House of Commons and later became distinguished statesmen, I note in the foremost ranks the names of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Georges E. Cartier. Why have these men played such an important part in history? It is because they always recognized and respected the rights of the minority. May I recall to your memory a splendid speech delivered in the house by Sir John A. Macdonald, in which he stated:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other; I believe that would be impossible if it were tried and it would be foolish and wicked' if it were possible. The statement that has been made so often that this is a conquered country is "a propos de

rien." Whether it was conquered or ceded we have a constitution under which all British subjects are in a position of absolute equality, having rights of every kind, of language, of religion, of property and of person. There is no paramount race in this country, there is no conquered race in this country, we are British subjects and those who are not English are none the less British subjects on that account.
I do not wish to rouse any racial prejudices; however, I put the question to the house, whether this right is embodied in our constitution. Why then not apply it to help the " bonne entente " in all the provinces of confederation.
I recall that, in 1916, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) raised an interesting discussion in the house. The resolution he introduced became known as the ''Lapointe motion." I should like to see the former Minister of Justice in his seat so as to remind him that, on that occasion, I had the privilege of voting in favour of his resolution. This motion created quite a stir at the time and even brought fame to him.
Hon. gentlemen may perhaps contend that, those in favour of bilingualism last year, wanted the house to vote on the merit of this question; unfortunately, unforeseen events prevented the house from doing so. That is why I wished to remove from party strife, the question of bilingual currency, I was therefore in favour of a committee composed of fifteen members chosen among the leading members of the house. Hon. gentlemen will note that the opposition is represented by five former ministers. One cannot cast any doubt on the good intentions of the former Minister of Justice, no more than on those of the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). They are legal lights, known for their moral and social probity, which is an assurance that this question will be fairly dealt with and do full justice to the French Canadian element of this country. Thus will disappear all friction which may exist between majority and minority groups.
If one inquires why the question is left to a committee, it is because each time the house was called upon to consider resolutions of that kind, the various groups in the house always made political capital by appealing each time to race prejudice and thus preventing the success of our cause. The committee will be authorized to take down the evidence of persons not connected with the house; such as bank managers, officials of the Finance department, etc.
These are reasons which certainly favoured the appointment of a committee.
Furthermore, I wish to point out to the house that never has a political party been

Bilingual Currency-Mr. Boulanger
able to hoist itself into office by appealing to racial prejudices, and that never will a party hold office by bringing up such questions. I would like to see all my friends present here so as to warn them well, that never a political party will assume power without having the support of the province of Quebec. In 1911, that province gave 27 seats to the Conservative party. In 1921, the Liberal party took office with 65 seats from Quebec, and in 1930, the Conservative party returned to power with 25 members from Quebec. This goes to prove that Quebec is closely linked with smooth and good government. Each time a party takes office, Quebec will greatly be interested, because she will always be the province that has placed that party in office.
If I had a suggestion to make to members on the committee, it would be the following: Let them bear in mind the prayer which they repeat together every day before each sitting of the house, when they implore the Almighty for peace and harmony. I trust that this idea of the " bonne entente " will bear abundant fruit and thus contribute to the welfare of the Canadian people.
Mr. OSCAR L. BOULANGER (Belle-chasse) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I wish
to congratulate the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette) on his comments generally replete with common sense. I must also thank him for his kind references to me. His kindness makes me regret more so that I find it impossible to entirely approve the measure he has submitted to the house. I would be inclined to vote in favour of this resolution if it could bring some result. I may say further: I would even support the measure were I convinced that it would do no harm. Unfortunately, in spite of all the eloquence of my hon. friend, the member for Berthier-Maskinonge, he has not convinced me that his motion would not be harmful.
He requests the appointment of a committee to consider the question whether we should have in this county bilingual currency. I think that this question is no longer debatable. It has been settled. French Canadians, at all events, consider that the question has been definitely settled long ago. By his resolution, my hon. friend from Berthier Maskinonge brings up again the whole question and re-opens the discussion. May I point out, sir, that the question the hon. member wishes a committee to examine is purely and simply a question of law, it is not one of fact. There is no need of witnesses to establish whether we are entitled or not to speak French in Canada or whether we are entitled to have public documents published in the French language. There is nothing to establish, nothing to prove, the question is purely and simply a constitutional one. I even think that it would even be, so to speak, humiliating to have a committee of the house consider whether we are entitled to speak the French language or whether public documents should be published in French. As far as I am concerned and that includes many, the question was settled long ago, ever since we have a constitution and even long before, because the latter only sanctioned-and badly at that, in my opinion-the natural right of one-third of the population of Canada to read in its own language the public documents of this nation

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
If there be a public document which expresses the character of a nation, it is certainly currency. There should be no opposition against the language of one-third of the population- especially when it is that of the pioneers of this country, of those who discovered Canada, civilized and defended it against the invader -being placed on our currency.
My hon. friend stated a moment ago: This is not a new question, for ever so long has it been threshed out in parliament. He mentioned the name of my hon. friend from Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne), whom I regret not to see in the house because he is unable to leave his room owing to illness. Then, if the question has been discussed so much in parliament, if it has been the topic for so many years, it is futile to further study it, to appoint a committee so as to again consider and inquire into a matter which is so well known, since it has been before the house for a score of years. No good result will ensue from the appointment of this committee and the question would remain unsettled.
I am quite aware that my hon. friend, the member for Berthier-Maskinonge is sincere in his endeavours; I do not question his good intentions. However, I fully know that the fact of referring .a question to a committee is the usual way of side tracking it. I quite understand that if a first-class funeral is contemplated for an embarrassing question, a committee of the house is appointed to study the matter. I am aware of my hon. friend's intentions and the object he has in mind, nevertheless the only practical result of his motion, if adopted, will be to postpone the question; it will once more be sidetracked and buried. What we want, is not the study of a question already under consider-

Bilingual Currency-Mr. Boulanger
ation for a score of years, it is not more light on a subject which has often been discussed in the house, what we want is action, the settling of this question, once for all, so that nothing more will be heard about it. We demand the acknowledgment of the principle that Canada is a bilingual country, and that the act which governs our metal currency and notes being, by virtue of our constitution, printed and promulgated in both languages, our currency must necessarily also be stamped or printed in the two languages.
When this question is settled, once for all, nothing further will be heard about it, we shall have peace and harmony which my hon. friend mentioned just now. The best way of obtaining peace, order and harmony in this country, is by respecting the rights and privileges of all citizens. To my mind, it is not requesting too much to claim that the Trench language, one of the two official languages of this country, should appear on such an official document as our currency. Therefore, sir, so as to prevent that this motion be adjourned or again side-tracked, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier) the following amendment to the resolution of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge:
That the resolution be amended by striking out all the words after "be" in the third' line and substituting in place thereof: "settled once for all and that the government should immediately take the necessary steps to conform itself to our constitution in this respect."
I have but little to add to what the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge has stated just now as to the merit of the question, or to what was said last year in the house by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre).
Bilingual currency is not an extraordinary departure, it exists in half the countries of the world. In Switzerland the money is struck in the three official languages of the country, in Italian, French and German; the currency is bilingual in Belgium, while in India, Ceylon, the Dutch Indies, Tunis, Indo China, Nigeria, in short, I might say, in half the countries of the world they have bilingual currencies. Even in Japan and certain provinces of China, currency is bilingual, not because those countries are bilingual, but in order to accommodate every one. Money is stamped both in English and Japanese, in Japan, and in Chinese and English in certain provinces of China.

For all these reasons, I move the amendment I have just read.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks may I say that it is my intention to make them as dispassionate and to remain as cool headed as I possibly can. In my opinion, however, there are some truths that must be told, and I intend to tell them.
When my hon. friend from Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette) prepared this motion, and I think before he sent it to the clerk of the house, he was kind enough to write and ask me if I would like my name to appear as the mover. I declined, but when he asked me to second the resolution I gladly accepted. May I say that one of my principal reasons for refusing to move the resolution was that I have lived long enough to have a certain knowledge of human nature, and I knew full well that if I moved the resolution my motives and intentions would be misinterpreted. On the other hand, due to what has taken place in the house since I made mjr remarks on this question last year, and due also to what has happened outside of this chamber, I was very glad to have the opportunity to say a word or two in this connection.
I said just a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, that I knew that if I moved the resolution my intentions would be misinterpreted. I may add that in a great many cases the intentions of public men are more or less suspected, and in my opinion there are many reasons for that state of affairs. To my mind there is no doubt that the deeds of a few public men in the past have had something to do with the spread of this sentiment among the people, and it may very well be that the party press have had a good deal to do with it also. I do believe, however, that the politicians themselves have had a great deal to do with it. I do not mean to say that they have been deceiving the public, but they have brought about that attitude by their lack of sincerity on public matters. I hold in my hand a newspaper containing a letter or an article written by an hon. member of this house.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: What newspaper is that?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
It was copied by several newspapers; the one I have is Le Devoir of November 9. The article was written by the deputy speaker of this house, the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne), and is entitled Le Rouge et le Bleu, or the Red and the Blue. Time will not permit me to read

Bilingual Currency-Mr. Gobeil
this article, but anyone reading it must arrive at t'he conclusion that since confederation French Canadian public men in the province of Quebec have betrayed their nationality and their race. I want to protest against this suggestion, because I do not think it is borne out by the facts. I do not believe our public men coming from the province of Quebec have been traitors to their race; I believe they hav"e done their best. I know they have not been able to attain their desires in all ways, but it is very regrettable that such statements as are made in this article should be made by a public man of our province.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: What is the statement? Would the hon. gentleman read it?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: No, it is too long. Anyone can read it. I am not blaming the newspaper; the article appeared in several newspapers in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but having referred to that article I think he should read the statement which he says was made by an hon. member of this house.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
I want to illustrate what I have just said, Mr. Speaker, by a quotation I gave last year when I spoke on the bilingual resolution. I reminded the house of the remarks made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1907. Speaking on February 27 of last year I quoted Sir Wilfrid Laurier as follows:
But I must protest against the idea that because bank notes are not printed in French as well as English, one can state that the French language is not on a footing of equality with the English.
We have our rights and we should exercise them when it is our interest to do so, but I do not think we should be pedantic and insist that on every occasion the French language should be spoken.
Permit me, Mr. Speaker, to add to this another paragraph of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's speech.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me juist a question?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: I am sorry, but I have not time. If the hon. member wishes to speak he will have an opportunity.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: What is that quotation from?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
It is a quotation from a speech by Sir Wilfrid Laurier delivered in the
House of Commons on February 25, 1907. He continued:
But to affirm, as he does-
Referring to the hon. member for Mont-magny.
-that the French language should be used upon every occasion, and that every public document should be printed on one side in French and the other side in English, is, I think, going a little too far. For instance, I understand that my hon. friend wants bank notes to be printed either in French or in English. For my part I never yet saw an occasion where a bank note printed in English was not properly understood by the French people; and I am quite sure that a bank note printed in French would be understood by the English people to be exactly what it means. But I see no reason why a bank note should not be printed in French.
At the end of his remarks, Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved the following amendment:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted in place thereof:
"The Freueh language is, in fact, as well as by the constitution, on a footing of equality with the English language."
When last year I quoted these words from Sir Wilfrid Laurier I asked hon. members opposite to rise from their seats and tell this House of Commons, tell the province of Quebec and tell the country, whether Sir Wilfrid Laurier was a traitor to his nationality when he used those words. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what would have happened last year to the humble member for Oompton, or, for that matter, to any hon. member on this side of the house, if we had made a declaration of that kind. If I am to judge by what the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Ohevrier) said, when he spoke after me last year, I think I should probably have been lynched, had I made such a declaration, I well remember what I said; I pronounced myself in favour of the motion. I did not believe that at the time it was wise for this chamber to vote on the matter, and I have not changed my opinion. I still believe it is not a wise move to have a vote on this matter.
Referring to me the hon. member for Ottawa said:
It would have been better for this gentleman if he had never seen light.
Mr. Speaker, what would have been my fate if I had made a declaration such as Sir Wilfrid Laurier made in 1907? Was Sir Wilfrid Laurier a traitor? I am sorry to say that not one member opposite had courage to rise and vindicate the memory of his leader-not one of them, not even the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) who is not in his seat to-day. I say he should be

Bilingual Currency-Mr. Gobeil
in the house 'because he knew this motion was coming up for consideration. Not even the hon. member for Quebec East had the courage to rise and state in this chamber whether or not he believed Sir Wilfrid Laurier was or was not a traitor.
Let me tell the house what I think-and I am doing this to illustrate a point I made a few minutes ago: I consider Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not a traitor to his nationality when he made that declaration. But, knowing what he knew and knowing that it was not possible for him to give bilingual currency at the time, he had the courage to get up and to state, not the reasons why he could not do it -because he was then Prime Minister-but to make the declaration to which I have referred. I think we as French Canadians should not consider that man a traitor to his nationality and to his race who, while leader of his party, made this declaration.
Let us come a little nearer to the year 1933, which we have been discussing. May I remind hon. members of what happened in 1929? In 1929 the contract for the printing of Canadian currency, Canadian bank notes, had to be renewed. Every hon. member in this chamber knows the party which at that time held office. Accidentally or otherwise,- I am not in a position to say-during the six months preceding the renewal of the contract 34S petitions were sent from every corner of this dominion to the Minister of Finance asking for bilingual currency. What happened, Mr. Speaker? The contract was renewed. At that time hon. members from the province of Quebec were on this side of the house, but not one of them said a word; not one raised his voice. Even the hon. member for Quebec East, who was the leader of the members from that province, and acted as their tactician, did not see fit to raise his voice in answer to those petitions.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Not even the hon. member for Temiscouata.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
No, not one of them. I want to be fair to hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not even blame them; I do not blame them because they did not give this country bilingual currency. I feel certain they did not do it because they could not do it. I know my hon. friends opposite well enough to know that they love their nationality and their language, and if it had been possible to convince the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) the then Prime Minister, to give bilingual currency to Canada, they would have done it. But they could not do it, and I could not blame them for that. What I do blame them for, however, is their lack 
of sincerity when, in 1933, they came to this House of Commons and moved a resolution such as that which stood in the name of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger). The position hon. members opposite took last year has given the public the impression that they cannot rely upon their representatives in the House of Commons.
As I said at the beginning I do not wish to be unfair. I do believe however that there are some truths which should be told, and I intend to tell them. I wish to make a very definite statement, or accusation, if you choose to use that word-I will use the word statement. I want to say that the Liberal party of the province of Quebec, headed by the hon. member for Quebec East, last year induced the hon. member for Bellechasse to move his resolution for no other purpose than to derive political advantage.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: I rise to a point of order, Mr. Speaker. It is a very well known rule of the house that an hon. member has no right to impute motives to another hon. member, and I would ask that the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) withdraw the statement he has just made.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: I have no objection at all, Mr. Speaker, I will put it in another way.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. He must withdraw it entirely.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: I withdraw it with pleasure. Let me give the house an example of the sincerity of hon. gentlemen opposite. Did they know or did they not know that the contract was going to be renewed in 1929? Did they know that a central bank was coming sooner or later? I accuse the Liberal party of the province of Quebec, and more particularly the hon. member for Quebec East, because he is their leader, of moving the resolution last year for no other purpose than to place the government of the day in the position of having to face an adverse vote of the house so that the government could not put into effect what they failed to do in 1929.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I make the same objection to that remark.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had this information from a very reliable source when I spoke last year, but I did not want to use it because I wanted to give hon. gentlemen opposite a chance to vindicate their position and to vindicate their leader. Does the house want additional proof? All that hon. members have to do is to read the speech made by the hon. member for Bellechasse. Here is an hon. member of this house who comes

Bilingual Currency-Mr. Gobeil
before this chamber and asks its members to support his motion, and he cannot finish his speech without insulting them.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: My speech is in Hansard and it speaks for itself, and the hon. member for Compton has no right to put any such construction upon my words. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to ask him to withdraw.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Belle-chasse is not the one to decide whether his speech was offensive. I say that every member on this side or on the other side of the house who did not believe as he did and who did not belong to the same race as he did felt himself insulted, whether the hon. member for Bellechasse meant it or not. As he very well said, his speech speaks for itself.
My hon. friends opposite like very much to pose as champions of the rights of the French race and of the French language, and sometimes even of the Catholic church. Let me suggest to them that if they have at heart, as they claim, the interests of the French race, there are other fields of activity where they can exercise their energy to much better advantage for their race than on this question of whether or not we shall have bilingual currency in 1933, 1934 or 1940. When I say 1933 or 1940, I say it for a purpose.
May I address myself for a moment more particularly to my English speaking colleagues of this house? It is hardly necessary for me to say to the house that I am no lawyer. We have had lots of talk this year and last year about the British North America Act in connection with this matter. Some people claim that according to that act we have the legal right to have bilingual currency in this country, while others claim that we have not. I do not care that about the British North America Act.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
I simply appeal to common sense. I look at this question in a common sense way. Here we are a country of ten million people, over three million' of whom are of the French Canadian race. Those are the facts whether we have a right to bilingualism or not. I do not suspect for one minute that my English speaking friends are going to start a crusade and have all French Canadians slaughtered to get rid of them-not for one minute-and I am equally sure that the French Canadians have not the slightest thought of doing that to their English speaking compatriots. I am simply saying that, whether we like it or not, in this country
of ten million people, over three million are of the French Canadian race, and in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is a bilingual country and will remain a bilingual country for years to come. We have, it seems to me, certain rights over other minorities that might exist in this country because we are the first inhabitants of its soil. So why not make this country a real bilingual country? I think it would be to the advantage of all of us to have this country recognized as a bilingual country. As Sir Wilfrid Laurier so well said, where is the French Canadian who objects to an English two-dollar bill? And where is the English speaking Canadian in this chamber or outside who would object to a Dominion of Canada bill printed in French? There is not one I am sure, and so I appeal to our English speaking friends on both sides of, the house, and ask them to accede to the wish of one-third of the population of this country and give the French Canadians bilingual bills, if you like, although I do not care to mention bilingual bills particularly. Rather I say let us make this country a real bilingual country because it is bound to remain so for generations and generations to come.
My time is flying, Mr. Speaker, and as I can speak faster in French I will conclude my remarks in that language.
(Translation): I was stating, sir, that if hon. members opposite have truly at heart the interest of their race or nationality, there are for them matters of greater importance than this question of bilingual currency which will come up and is bound to come up in the near future.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: If this question is of minor importance why do you second the motion.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: I would suggest to them, sir, if they are so anxious to work in the interest of their race, to travel down in groups to Quebec, so as to request the government of that province to see that the chairman of the two most important committees of the Legislative Assembly be French Canadians instead of being Jews; in the only Catholic province of Canada, as the Hon. Mr. Taschereau delights in calling it.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
That has
nothing to do with the question.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
I would
request them to use their influence with the Quebec government so that the latter may set aside for the citizens of that province what is left of our natural resources.

Bilingual Currency-Mr. Gobeil

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: That is irrelevant.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: -instead of continuing to alienate them to give them away for a pottage of lentils.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Who is the
lunatic (aliene) ?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
If the Quebec government, sir, had had at heart the interests of the Quebec people, if our friends had at heart the interests of their fellow-citizens, what good work they could have accomplished! Instead of allowing the names of cabinet ministers of that province to appear on the prospectus of fraudulent companies which exploit the farming class, making use as they do of the names of these ministers to palm off worthless shares, the government of my province should have directed the small savings of our people towards such sound investments as our natural resources. If these hon. gentlemen are so anxious, let them show it by working in the interest of their race; I would advise them to go to Montreal-
' An hon. MEMBER (Translation):	We
shall pay a visit to the people of Compton at the next election.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: -in order to interview the administrators of the university of Montreal-I mean the lay administrators, not the church authorities, who were made ushers, but the lay administrators themselves, or liberal laymen in charge-so as to use their influence to induce them to expel from the university the anti-jewish element which is contaminating our young men.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: The antijewish element, hear, hear!

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Let them
expel from the university the professors who are atheists, those who have no god and who take upon themselves to educate and form the minds of our youth.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: You are an expert on jam, but when it comes to poetry you are a failure!

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
My hon.
friend, reminds me-

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: You had better not speak about it. You will get all muddled up.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
My hon. friend reminds me of a fable of Lafontaine: An old cunning fox having had the misfortune of losing his tail in a trap, gathered all the foxes
IMr. Gobeil.]
of the surrounding country and, with his back turned to the wall, made them a splendid speech so as to persuade them to dispense with that appendix which, in his opinion, only served to sweep the dust of roads.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: You do not like foxes because they do not feed on jam, they are not clients of your brother.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
The hon. member has never expressed his views on the bilingual question and he would like to see his fellow-citizens do likewise.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): He never speaks!

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: We were ready to vote and you have prevented us.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Had I a suggestion to make to the hon. member, it would be that he should study this fable of Lafontaine and ponder over the fate of this poor fox when his congeners noticed that he had lost his tail.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): Oh! Oh!
Mr: GOBEIL (Translation): I would request you, sir, to maintain order, if you please.
(Text) The ACTING SPEAKER (Mr. Morand): Order!

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
I am aware,
sir, that I have shocked a few in my remarks. I heard certain comments, made by my hon. friends opposite, that this had nothing to do with the question. I beg to differ. I contend that the reason set forth by our hon. friends toward proceeding with last year's motion, was the interest they display on behalf of the people of their province; however, I can show that there are other problems than that of bilingual currency in which they can be of more service to their fellow citizens. I appeal to the educated class, to professional men, on both sides of the house, and I ask them if, frankly, they have well fulfilled their duty as citizens, they that have the task, as the elite of the people, to guide public opinion in Quebec.
May I quote, sir, a small excerpt from Cardinal Villeneuve's speech delivered a few days ago in Montreal.
It is as follows:
Gentlemen, our universities must raise the level of their religious teaching. The various faculties should be replete with it for the sake of Catholic dignity and elementary logic. Have we Catholic universities where students may graduate as lawyers or physicians, just as they would graduate elsewhere, yes or no?

Bilingual Currency-Mr. Mercier (Laurier)
I think, what I request, sir, from professional men in this house, is only rational. I state that it is incumbent on our universities, on the university of Montreal to prepare our young men for their future callings, and if our country is to emerge from this crisis without the convulsions experienced by other countries, it will be due to the Christian spirit, religious spirit and common sense taught to our youth. Is it rational, reasonable and fair to send our young men of 14, 15, to 20 years, to an institution where they are contaminated by anti-Christian, and anti-French Canadian surroundings-
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): Where?
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): In what institution?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
At the university of Montreal-and where professors, I repeat it, atheist professors, anti-religious professors are permitted to give their lectures.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): Are there professors who are atheists in the university of Montreal?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Yes, there are.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): Name them.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
It is unnecessary to name them, they are well known.
This bilingual question is very interesting, indeed, to us French Canadians, however, there are other spheres where we can be more useful and render better services, because bilingual currency will come sooner or later, but better soon than later.
I have myself a son who attended lectures at the university; I also have another who will probably attend them in a few years.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Has he come out contaminated?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
No he did not, because I did not send him to the university of Montreal. I would not care to send him there nor shall I send him there, unless things change.
Mr. MERCIER (St. Henri), (Translation): Where did you send him to the Swiss school?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Laval university, in Quebec.
This, sir, practically closes the remarks that I intended to make on the motion of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette). I did not dwell very much on the merit of the motion itself, as to whether it will settle the problem or not. I must frankly confess that I am not fully convinced that this resolution will be the means of establishing a bilingual currency or preventing it.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Is that why you seconded the motion?

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: I seconded the motion, sir, because I wished to show to my province-

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: Dirt thrown on the university of Montreal!

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
-the insincerity of the position taken by members of the opposition on this question.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): It is a pity if you are in earnest.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
I stated that I was not fully convinced that this resolution would give the country a bilingual currency. I am convinced, however, that we shall have it without this motion; I moreover think that this bilingual currency would come even if the motion of the hon. member for Belle-chasse had not been introduced last year.
So as not to question, sir, the sincerity of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge- and I neither question it-I shall support this resolution if a vote is asked, although as I have just stated, I am not quite convinced that it will improve matters. As an hon. member opposite has just asked why I spoke on this motion, I shall state that I wanted to make clear the attitude I took last year, when a vote was taken on this question; furthermore, that I have not since changed my views and 'that I think, as I then thought, that the house should not be called upon to vote on this question.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in this debate but when the hon. member for BeMechasse (Mr. Boulanger) put my name to his amendment, it necessarily fell to my lot to say a word or two. After the remarks of the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) it became more incumbent on me or some hon. member on this side of the house to say something. The hon. gentleman who preceded me stated his remarks in a very benign manner and although he did not make himself absolutely clear as to his intentions in connection with the motion before the house, I think we can take it that he is in favour of a bilingual currency in this country. We on this side are in favour of such a currency, not as a matter of begging but as a matter of right.
There is a certain fact which is so selfevident that I hardly think I need mention it to hon. members, but for the sake of my argument I refer hon. members to section 133 of the British North America Act. This section recognizes the fact that there are two
970	COMMONS
Bilingual Currency-Mr. Mercier (Laurier)
languages in this country and states that either the English or the French language may be used in the debates of the houses of parliament as well as in the houses of the legislature of the province of Quebec. This section likewise recognizes the right to the use of both official languages in the records and journals of parliament. Under this section it is also given to the people of Canada to plead before the courts of the country in the language in which they are accustomed to express themselves.
The hon. member for Compton sidestepped the issue when he went back to that state of mind for which he is well known and attempted to abuse hon. members on this side for certain happenings last year. If the house will remember, the hon. member for Bellechasse moved a motion asking this house to decide that it was the right of a certain section of the Canadian population to have a bilingual currency. After a protracted discussion the hon. member for Compton moved a motion to give the resolution of the hon. member for Bellechasse the six months' hoist.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CURRENCY, STATE NOTES AND BONDS STAMPED AND PRINTED IN THE TWO OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
I stand corrected. His motion was that the debate be adjourned, and later the debate went on and the question was talked out. Now this year the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge, whether he recognizes the principle of the resolution or not, comes forward with a resolution to the effect that this question should be submitted to a special committee consisting of certain hon. members. 'Well, we say that either this question is worthy of consideration or it is not. I have just said that the French language is recognized under the British North America Act, and we well remember that under the previous administration the same difficulties arose that are arising here to-night. It is quite true that section 91 of that act commits to the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada the subject of currency and coinage. But turning to section 133, to which my hon. friend was referring, one sees that if from the first section I have named any deduction were to be drawn as to the resolution now before the house, the matter in question is governed by section 133, which clearly and expressly sets forth the position in regard to language in this country. Section 133, which my hon. friend did not read, is as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and botli those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
I do not ask the house to accept my opinion as one on which the subject is to be decided; but it does seem to me that you have in that section a clear definition of the occasions on which the different languages may be used. It is directed to the use of the two languages not only in the courts and houses of parliament of Canada and legislature of Quebec but also in the respective records and journals of those houses and in pleading or process in the courts. And lest it be thought that perhaps printing might include something in the na-

The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
That is, it is confined, as far as printing is mentioned, to the acts of the legislature of the province of Quebec and the parliament of Canada.
That act, Mr. Speaker, is almost a legislative bargain; it was at all events the result of an agreement arrived at in the year 1867 between elements that perhaps at times were rather in conflict. It is not an act with which all the people in my province are satisfied. But it is an act under which people in my province have lived and acted and carried on their business and affairs, political or otherwise, not because they liked it in some instances, but because they had said they would do it, and they proposed to stick with their bargain and follow the provisions of this act.
I must say that last year the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) did not approach this subject in a way calculated to induce that friendly feeling which we think should obtain amongst us, because at the beginning of his address and at the end of it he used language of a highly provocative nature, language which I resented at the time but of which I did not think I should take notice. It seemed to me that I should almost lower myself by taking advantage of the opportunity then afforded to me and expressing resentment of it in words. The hon. gentleman, opening his speech at that time-the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) referred to it, and I have here a copy of the speech-said he had hopes of convincing people whom he described in very laudatory terms but he had no hope of convincing ignorant or bigoted or silly people. Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is room in all kindliness, in all confraternity, for differences of opinion; but to describe those who venture to differ from the hon. gentleman by such words as those was, as I say, provocative rather than conciliatory, and did not tend, had we chosen to take it that way, to promote the good feeling of the debate. Then he ended by addressing hon. members of this house, if you please, as "hare brained people of the Orange Order, who have brought into this free and peaceful country the narrow and ignorant fanaticism of foreign countries." I took no notice of it; neither did any other hon. member of the house that I know of, but I draw attention to it now because the hon. gentleman spoke of it, and I say it is not conciliatory language, not the kind of language to address to any

hon. member of this house. Yet the hon. member closed his speech upon the resolution by using just those words.
The hon. member for Laurier-0ut remonit (Mr. Mercier) says it is provided in the British North America Aot that there should be this use of the two languages. If it were so I would not be one to raise a finger against it. I miight diisiliike it intensely-I do not as a matter of fact-but I would not raise my hand or my voice in gesture or whisper against what is the law, much as I or as anyone might feel that he was opposed to it. But then my friends say:	"Be agreeable; give us a concession". They treat it as though it were something we should agree to and hand to them. But, Mr. Speaker, I am not warranted in doing that. I respect the opinions of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this resolution on the other side of the house; as far as I understood them I respect entirely the views they express. Mr. JOHN A.SULLIVAN (St.Ann): Mr. Speaker, I have not spoken in this house very often. I am sure that was not his meaning, because we on this side of the house believe that the university of Montreal is certainly worthy of the French Canadian race, of the province of Quebec and of Canada.
I want to add just a few words. My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary) said the British North America Act did not give us the right to have bilingual currency in Canada. Possibly this is true in the strict letter of the law, but at the present time everyone is asking for an amendment to the British North America Act. This government can do anything it wishes except change a man into a woman. If this right does not exist under the British North America Act, I ask the house to pass a resolution ateking for an amendment of that act so that we may have bilingual currency in this country.
In order to understand the situation we must study the history of Canada, which was ceded to Great Britain in 1763. The battle of the Plains of Abraham took place in 1759; Canada was surrended in 1760, and finally the Treaty of Paris was signed in 1763. At that time there were sixty thousand French Canadians living in this country; in 1774 there were about one hundred thousand, while there were only five or six hundred English people in Canada. Sir Guy Carleton, later Lord Dorchester, one of the greatest men in history, certainly understood the situation. Sir Guy Carleton, governor of Canada, went to England and explained the situation in this country to the British parliament. It is one of the miracles of history that the British people, after having failed to keep in one community those of

I say without fear of contradiction, and history will prove my contention, that Lord Dorchester, by obtaining for Canada the Quebec Act of 1774, performed the greatest service that could have been performed for this country and the British Empire. That act gave to the French Canadians the right to follow their own religion and to be governed by their own civil laws; it gave the priests the right to exercise their ministry; and that act kept the French Canadians together when Canada was attacked by the United States. Mr. Speaker, I beg the indulgence of the house for a few moments. First let me say, however, that in view of the fact that my hearing is not as good as it might be I did not hear everything said by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil). Nevertheless, Whatever his expression of opinion might have been, I feel I must dissociate myself from any criticism against the distinguished personnel of the university of Montreal for Whom, in Quebec, irrespective of any party affiliations, we have nothing but the greatest admiration and respect.
Sometimes it is sickening and discouraging when, on occasions when French Canadians on both sides of the house ought to present a united front in order to appeal to the sense of justice of the majority of Canadians, we lose our time and discredit ourselves by hurling insults at each other and indulging in personalities which, on occasions, call for action by Mr. Speaker. We ought not to resurrect old party quarrels; as I have said, We ought to be united in asking from the majority in this House of Commons a recognition of the letter of the British North America Act and, if not the letter at least the spirit. (Because, as has been said, sometimes when the letter is not dear the spirit vivifies.

I must disapprove of the expression of opinion voiced to-night by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) who stated that he is not ready to make concessions. I think we ought to rise to higher ground. Listening to such statements from him I remembered that only on Saturday last, the day before yesterday, there was invited to the city of Quebec a distinguished educationalist from the university of Toronto, Mr. Dunlop, director of public relations, who appeared before the Canadian Club on Saturday afternoon and pleaded for cooperation between the Canadian races, and the recognition of the French language in Canada. He stated that in the university of Toronto lessons are given in the French language not only by distinguished French speaking professors from Canada but by professors from Paris. He stated that over the radio inter-university debates are being held in the French language between the university of Toronto and universities in the province of Quebec. He stated, further, that this week there would be a bilingual debate between the students of the university of Winnipeg, Manitoba, and those of Laval university at Quebec.
If we were basing our contentions only on the letter of the British North America Act, would we be on safe ground? I say yes, but I understand some people might say no. I repeat we ought not only to look at the letter of the contract, but we must also look at the spirit of it. Let us take inspiration from the eloquent words expressed in the Canadian House of Commons in 1890 by one of the greatest of the men who have led the Conservative party, Sir John A. Macdonald. His words are as follows:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in certain quarters that by any mode whatever there should' be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to make it inferior to the other.
I believe that would be impossible if it were tried, and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible. The statement that has been made so often that this is a conquered country is "a propose de rien." Whether it was conquered or ceded we have a constitution under which all British subjects are in a position of absolute equality, having equal rights of every kind, of language, of religion, of property, of person.
There is no paramount race in this country. There is no conquered race in this country, we are all British subjects and those who are not English are none the less British subjects on that account.	,
Let us be inspired by the words of Sir John A. Macdonald; let us discuss and study the rights of the French language on a broad and higher plane. In that respect, Mr. FEBRUARY 26, 1934
