Mr. Speaker, some comment has been made regarding the fact that I spoke on a similar motion a year ago. If I remember the circumstances correctly, we have spent at least ninety-five per cent of the time allotted to this debate in listening to hon. members from the province of Quebec, and it does seem strange if one English speaking person from the rest of Canada should not be allowed five or ten minutes to express his views, without being subjected to criticism. My hon. friends opposite say: Why should this matter have been talked out-as they call it-in 1933, when they were anxious to have a vote? Why was it necessary to wait until 1933 to have their great anxiety satisfied? Where were those hon. gentlemen between the years 1905 and 1911? Where were they and their predecessors in this house? Where were hon. gentlemen opposite and their predecessors between 1922 and 1929, if they were so anxious to have this legislation passed? Why did they wait until 1933 to bring the matter up?
If I have time I shall refer to some of the remarks made by their leaders, with respect to action lion, gentlemen have taken in the debate this evening and in that of 'last year. I want to say this, that so far as I could judge the debate this evening, with my limited knowledge of the French language-I shall read it to-morrow morning and get it more clearly-it seemed to me more like a political fight among members from the province of Quebec as to who would get the most kudos from the province of Quebec for raising this question. If there had been any great desire to have this legislation passed in days gone by, it would have been shown by the action of hon. members. I should like to place on record the action taken in 1905 by the Liberal party with respect to this very question. I am sorry the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not in his seat. It is a matter of comment that he has not been here this evening to listen to the debate. I am sorry also that the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) who is said to be the champion of the French speaking people, is not in his seat to-night.
The matter was formally raised on May 21, 1905, and is reported at page 6826 of Hansard
for that year. Further reference to the matter was made by the hon. member for Montmagny in the debate which took place in the session of 1906-7. I wish to place on record questions asked of the government of which Sir Wilfrid Laurier was leader, and which had his approval, or they would not have been, placed on Hansard. The answers were given by Mr. W. S. Fielding, the then Minister of Finance. The questions are in these terms:
1.	Do any grave reasons of state exist that might prevent the Minister of Finance from having the dominion one dollar and two dollar notes or all other bank notes printed simultaneously in English and French?
2.	Are they unaware in the Finance department that the two languages are official in Canada?
3.	Is it the intention of the Minister of Finance to rectify in the future this state of things by ordering that those bank notes be printed in both languages, English and French?
The answer by Mr. Fielding is as follows:
There is nothing in the British North America Act or in any act of the parliament of Canada which requires or contemplates the printing of dominion notes in two languages.
The Finance department has not contemplated the advisability of any departure from the practice which has existed under all governments from the beginning of confederation down to the present time.
That was the official statement of the Liberal party on this question in 1905. That position has not been departed from by the Liberal' party in this house since then. No matter what hon. gentleman opposite may say in this debate here to-night, they cannot convince their own party that the answer given in 1905 was wrong. They cannot get the support of their own members on this question and they probably owe me a debt of gratitude for talking till eleven o'clock so that the rest of the party will not be put on record on this question to-night.
There is only one solution of this question, Mr. Speaker, and that is the solution that I think was suggested by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) to-night, the resolution he might have suggested last year, and that is that the government of this country in the printing of bills, notes, currency and all these other departmental forms follow the constitution of this country and the British North America Act. If it is necessary to find out what the British North America Act means, there are ways and means of doing so. I maintain that whatever rights the French language has in this dominion there is not the right to have pieces of paper printed by this government with both French and English on it. There is the right to have the statutes printed in French; there is the right
976	COMMONS
Bilingual Currency-Mr. Turnbull
to have the statutes printed in English, but there is no right to have a bilingual set of statutes. There may be a right under the act to have bills printed in French; there may be a right under the act to have bills printed in English; but there can be no two questions about it that there is no right under the act to have bills printed in both English and French-that is bilingual bills. I am prepared to go further and say with regard to postage stamps, to which my hon. friend referred, and other departmental forms, that there is no legal right under the act to have them printed in the two languages. You may have French stamps; you may have English stamps; you may have French post office forms, or you may have English post office forms; but you have no right under the act to have them printed in both the English and the French language.
Whatever the British North America Act says, whatever the rights are under that, when they are decided upon I am prepared to abide by them. If they say we are to have bilingual currency, well and good. I do not wish to take from the French people one single jot or tittle of what was given them by the British North America Act. There is my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) who says: We want concessions if the British North America Act does not give us enough. Then there is my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) who says: No, we do not want any concessions; we only want what the act says. What are we to believe, Mr. Speaker, in regard to what they desire? Those are the two opinions that I heard expressed here during this debate.
Let me say that in speaking as I do tonight I am not one of those who were referred to in the debate a year ago by the hon. inember for Bellechasse; I am not one of the bigoted class. I do not belong to the Orange order; I do not belong to the Ku Klux Klan;
I do not belong to the Knights of Columbus, and I am not speaking as the representative of any one of them, I have the greatest admiration for them all, but I do not belong to any of them. I am speaking here as the member for the constituency of Regina, and expressing the views which the people of Regina would wish to have me express on this question which is before the house.
I have heard it said that the French language has rights in this country derived from treaties. I have looked at the Peace of Paris and at the terms of capitulation of 
Quebec and at the terms of capitulation of Montreal, and there is not one word in any of those three documents with regard to the use by the French speaking people of the French language in this country. So whatever rights the language might have in this country do not depend at all upon the terms of treaties or the terms of capitulation, but must rest upon statutory laws subsequently created by competent authority. As I say, in standing by the terms of the constitution, in standing by the terms of the British North America Act, I am in good company. .
And may I say that the feeling that exists in certain parts of Canada is not a feeling of resentment against the French language. In the province of Saskatchewan there is no person who would prohibit the use of the French language anywhere in the province by anyone who wants to use it. As a matter of fact, the provincial government is teaching the Frenph language both by correspondence and by lkssc>fs over the radio in the province of Saskatchewan, and yet Saskatchewan has been represented as the enemy of the French people. We do object to being made to use the French language, and we do object, owing to acts of administration by the government of this country, not this government, but previous governments, and this government as well, I might add, to being compelled to use the French language when we desire to use the English. With regard to post office forms in Saskatchewan, for instance, a French postinaster may send into the central office and get post office forms printed wholly in French. An English postmaster cannot send into the central office and get forms printed wholly in English. He has to take them in the two languages. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite from Quebec if they think that is fair. Then they ask us for further concessions. I say it is not fair. I say along with the leaders of both parties for many years that I stand by the constitution, and I think that is the only solution of this question we will ever get that will be a reasonable solution.
I want to refer in the few moments that are left to me to a resolution which was passed by the government of Canada and the opposition combined on the eighteenth day of February, 1890, which will be found in Hansard of that year at pages 881 and 882. Part of the resolution is in these words:
That, on the contrary, this house declares its adherence to the said covenants-

Canned Salmon Exports
That is, the covenants of the British North 'America Act:
-and its determination to resist any attempt to impair the same.
I stand in my place and say, as Sir John A. Macdonald said, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, as Sir John Thompson said, as the Hon. Edward Blake said, and as other great leaders of the Liberal party have said, that I adhere to the covenants of the British North America Act and to my determination to resist any attempt to impair them. That is the position I take here this evening.
